parties:
Abdul Aziz and others ------ Petitioners 
VS
Sahajuddin Mollah and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff petitioners is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Subordinate Judge Munshiganj on 6.6.90 in Title Appeal No. 28 of 1987 allowing the appeal, dismissing the original suit and setting aside the judgment and decree passed by Upazila Munsif (now Asstt. Judge) Tongibari on 25.3.87 in Title Suit No. 24 of 1984 decreeing the suit. 

 2. The petitioners being plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid Title Suit No. 24 of 1984 in the court of the Munsif, Tongibari upazila impleading the opposite parties as defendants for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession with respect to .05 decimals of land of the suit land as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the added defendant opposite parties contested the suit by filing separate written statements denying all material allegations made in the plaint with assertion that the suit is not maintainable in this present form and that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the suit land. 

 4. The learned Upazila Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Tongibari on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary decreed the Title Suit No. 24 of 1984 on contest. 

 5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the contesting opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 28 of 1987 and the learned Subordinate Judge, Munshiganj who heard the appeal by his judgment and decree allowed the appeal dismissing the original suit and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. 

 7. Mr. Md. Azizul Hoq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the appellate Court have categorically found that the learned Munsif committed an illegality in holding trial of the original suit which was beyond his pecuniary jurisdiction and, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is a nullity. He submits that when this is the finding it should go back to the trial Court for referring to a court having jurisdiction to try this case. I find substance in his submission. 

 10. In view of the discussions and the decision referred above I hold that both the judgments and decrees passed in Title Appeal No. 28 of 1987 and in Title Suit No. 24 of 1984 cannot be sustained in law and are liable to be set aside and are hereby set aside. The case is sent back on remand to the trial Court for trial of the suit by a proper court having pecuniary jurisdiction as was in the year 1984 as if the suit has been filed afresh there and shall proceed in accordance with law.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 8891 of 1991 (Dhaka).
Civil Revision No. 220 of 1989 (Rangpur).
parties:
Md. Abul Hossain and others.
Versus
Niranjon Mondal and others ------ Opp. Parties
full_judgment:
2. Short facts involved in the case are that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit being O.C. Suit No. 463 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif at Rajshahi Sadar for declaration that sale deed executed by Md. Ayub Ali Mondal (defendant No 4 of the suit) in favour of opposite parties is illegal, collusive, fraudulent, without consideration null and void having no legal effect and for a decree of declaration to the effect that the plaintiffs have their joint sixteen annas right, title and interest in the suit land and also for recovery of possession after evicting the defendants there from, that Haji Ayub Ali the defendant No. 4 in the suit got the property in suit by exchange who sold the same to the petitioners by registered deed, that subsequently the opposite parties purchased the land from Haji Ayub Ali the defendant No. 4 of the suit. 

 4. That thereafter the opposite parties filed an application under order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon which a Misc. Case being Misc Case No. 56 of 1984 was started and the opposite parties alleged in the Miscellaneous case under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure that no notice of the original suit was served upon them, that an appeal being the Appeal No. 190/X111/79-80 was pending before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) Rajshahi, amongst the parties, that the said appeal was fixed for hearing on 20.5.81 when it was disclosed that the petitioners got the suit land by dint of the ex parte decree from the Civil Court and in this way the opposite party No. 1 came to know about the ex parte decree, that after search the opposite parties finally come to learn on 30.5.1981 about the ex parte decree at Rajshahi Munsif's Court through their engaged lawyer, that the ex parte decree obtained by the petitioners is collusive, illegal and inoperative; that solenama filed by Haji Ayub Ali the defendant No. 4 in the original suit is also collusive, because Ayub Ali had been ill since 1 (one) year prior to passing of the decree and he had been bedridden, that Ayub Ali had no ability to put his thumb impression, that Gurupada opposite party No. 2 was not minor, that the petitioners contested the Miscellaneous Case for restoration under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by filing written objection denying all allegations brought by the opposite parties on the ground of maintainability, limitation and defect of parties etc. 

 5. That the case of the petitioners is that the opposite parties were well acquainted with the original suit as the notices and summons of the original suit were duly served upon them. The opposite parties have brought this false and concocted case only to harass these petitioners, that the petitioners took delivery of possession of the property in question in pursuance of the ex parte decree through the court on 18.4.1981 A. D. within the full knowledge of the opposite parties. That Haji Ayub Ali was not unable to put his L.T.I. on the said Solenama, that the false case of the opposite parties is liable to be rejected with costs. 

 6. That the learned Munsif, Nawabganj Sadar who heard the Miscellaneous Case rejected the same by the judgment and order dated 15.6.1986 in Miscellaneous Case No. 56 of 1984, with the finding that the petitioners had personal knowledge about the original suit and the summons thereof were duly served upon them. 

 8. That the learned Court of appeal below after considering the facts and circumstances in the case found that no notice had been directly served upon the defendants and the way the notices were served upon the defendants has been disbelieved. That in the application under Order 9 Rule 13 the main point involved is whether upon the defendants notices have been served properly or not and the learned appellate Court found that no notice was served upon the defendants directly and as such the serving of notices upon the defendants became doubtful and as regards the getting of possession of the suit lands through court on' the basis of compromise decree might be doubted as paper transaction and as such the learned Court of appeal below allowed the Miscellaneous Case and set aside the ex parte decree obtained by the plaintiff petitioners on 24.12.79 and 17.2.81 and the Court of appeal below was pleased to restore the original suit. 

 19. Considering the facts and circumstances involved in the case I do find that the defendant opposite parties should get a chance to contest the original suit to prove right and title in the suit land:-

full_judgment: Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: Defendant No. 5 is the petitioner and the matter arises from a suit relating to a property which the defendants claim to be a vested and non-resident property, leased out to Defendant No. 7. Plaintiffs-respondents claim title and possession of the land by Pattan from the admittedly original owner, Sunil Chandra Ghosh. But when defendant No. 7, claiming to be a lessee of the Government, threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession, they filed the suit in question (Title Suit No. 215 of 1984) for declaration of title and confirmation of possession, etc. The suit was decreed by the trial Court namely, the Assistant Judge, Manikganj, and his decision was upheld by the District Judge. Thereupon defendant No. 5, Additional Deputy Commissioner, Manikganj, challenged the decision in revision, (Civil Order No. 982 of 1991); but it was summarily dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned order dated 27 March, 1991. Petitioner is now seeking leave to appeal from the said order.

parties:
Shamima Khatoon and another   -------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others   -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
4. The respondent No. I, the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works contested the writ petition by filing affidavit-in-opposition wherein there has been general denial of the allegations made by the petitioners relating to the alleged contract of sale between the petitioner No. 1 and the original lessee and also relating to the alleged possession of the disputed house by the petitioners. The case of the contesting respondent appears to be that the original lessor of the disputed house being a Pakistani national and having left actually after liberation of Bangladesh the disputed house became abandoned property by operation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 hereinafter called PO 36 of 1972. As such, the Government took possession of the disputed house which was lying vacant and uncared for as abandoned property. Thereafter in pursuance of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 the disputed house was enlisted in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property in the official Gazette. According to the contesting respondent, the decision of the Court of Settlement refusing to exclude the disputed house from the 'Ka' list of abandoned property was fully justified and according to law. The contesting respondent also contends that the petitioners are not entitled to get possession in the disputed house. 

 5. Mr. MI Farooque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has first of all, tried to submit that the petitioner No. I acquired a legal right first of all by way of possession of the disputed house and accordingly, another right by entering into a contract of sale with the admitted original lessee and as such, she is entitled to enforce these rights against the respondent No. I who stepped into the shoes of the original owner after claiming the disputed house as vested property. Mr. Farooque has also argued that the Court of Settlement" did not consider this aspect of the case. Mr. Farooqui has not, however, seriously challenged the enlistment of the disputed house in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property by the respondent No. 1 by treating this property as abandoned property and his main contention has been that the petitioner No. I acquired a legal right on the basis of the contract of sale with the original lessee and in part performance of the contract the petitioner No. I being inducted into possession she is entitled to retain possession against the respondent No. 1 who by operation of PO 16 of 1972 stepped into the shoes of the original lessee. In support of his submission, Mr. Farooqui has placed reliance on a decision -of the Appellate Division of this Court in Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 266. 

 7. It is an admitted fact that the disputed house originally belonged to the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan and that it was leased out to one Md. Moinuddin by the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan by a deed of lease executed on 28.12.68 and registered on 30.12.68. It is also not disputed that the said Md. Moinuddin entered into possession of the disputed house. The petitioners allege that while in possession Md. Moinuddin entered into a contract of sale of the disputed house with the petitioner No. I for a consideration of Taka 7000.00 and executed a deed of agreement in her favour on receiving an advance payment of Taka 6001.00 stipulating to execute and register a deed of sale in due time after receiving the balance money. The contesting respondent in this writ petition has. tried to challenge the genuineness of the deed of agreement. We have perused the judgment of the Court of Settlement. A perusal of the judgment of the Court of Settlement as at Annexure F shows that such was taken by the respondent No. 1 at the Court of Settlement and the Court of Settlement found the deed of agreement to be a genuine document and proceeded to decide this case on this basis. This finding of fact that this deed of agreement was executed by the original lessee Md. Moinuddin arrived at by the Court of Settlement cannot again be raised and agitated before this court. It therefore, appears that there was an agreement between the original lessee Md. Moinuddin and the petitioner No. 1 on 13.10.70 for sale of the disputed house to her. The petitioners have also producted a General Power of Attorney as at Annexure C(I) to the writ petition. A perusal of the General Power of Attorney shows that the original lessee Md. Moinuddin authorised the petitioner No. 2 to deal with the disputed house including to transfer the disputed house by sale. It is admitted by the petitioners that till the filing of this writ petition the contract which was entered into between the petitioner No. 1 and the original lessee Md. Moinuddin was not specifically performed and no deed of sale was executed and registered in pursuance of the alleged contract as per the deed of agreement as at Annexure C to the writ petition. There is, therefore, no doubt that the title and ownership of the disputed house remained with the original lessee Md. Moinuddin when PO 16 of 1972 came into force on 10.3.73 i.e. the date of publication of this PO in the official Gazette. It is also admitted that the disputed house was enlisted in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property in pursuance of Ordinance No. LN of 1985 Section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 authorized the Government to publish a list of abandoned buildings in possession of the. Government In the writ petition it is admitted that the disputed house was being possessed by the Government and the petitioners were out of possession of the date on which PO 16 of 1972 came into force. It appears that by invokying section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 the Government enlisted the disputed house in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property vide notification in the official Gazette, Sub-section (2) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 provides as follows: 

 So by operation of sub-section (2) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 the publication of the disputed house in the official Gazette as abandoned property is conclusive evidence of the fact that the said house is abandoned property and has vested in the Government. The presumption flowing from sub-section (2) of section 5 of Ordinance LIV of 1985 that the Gazette notification showing enlistment of a house as an abandoned property is conclusive evidence that the said property is abandoned property and has vested in the Government is of course rebuttable and the persons interested are certainly entitled to rebut the presumption before a proper forum. We have perused the petition filed by the petitioners before the Court of Settlement and also the judgment of the Court of Settlement. The petition is at Annexure E to the writ petition and the judgment is at Annexure F to the writ petition. Since it is undisputed that the title and ownership of the disputed house remained with the original lessee Md. Moinuddin it was certainly necessary for the petitioners to adduce some evidence to show that the disputed house was not abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972 in order to rebut the presumption of conclusiveness of the evidence flowing from sub-section (2) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 to the effect that it was abandoned property. There is no statement in the petition filed by the petitioners in the Court of Settlement that the original lessee Md. Moinuddin with whom the ownership of the disputed house admittedly remained on the date of coming into force of PO 16 of 1972 did not answer to any of the ingredients which would render a property abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. The judgment passed by the Court of Settlement at Annexure F to the writ petition also discloses that the petitioners did not adduce any evidence to show that the original lessee Md. Moinuddin did not fall within the category of the persons whose property were to be abandoned property by operation of Article 2 of PO 16 of 1972. In fact we are satisfied that there was no attempt on the part of the petitioners to rebut the presumption of conclusiveness of evidence emanating from sub-section (2) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 before the Court of Settlement. Nor any attempt has been made by the petitioner to rebut the said presumption before this Court. So, since the presumption of conclusiveness of evidence flowing from the publication of the disputed house in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property in the official Gazette remains unrebuted we find that that Court of Settlement was justified in holding that the disputed house was rightly enlisted in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property. 

 8. Instead of seriously challenging the enlistment of the disputed houses abandoned property, Mr. Farooqui has strongly argued that after the property became abandoned this property vested in the Government by operation of Article 4 of PO 16 of 1972 and, as such, all the rights and liabilities of the original lessee Md. Moinuddin devalued on the Government. He has also elaborated his argument by contending that the petitioner No. I having been inducted into possession of the disputed house in part performance of the contract of sale entered between her and the original lessee Md. Moinuddin, the Government is bound to honour this contract and the petitioner No. I is entitled to protect her possession against the Government in view of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, As an authority for his proposition Mr. Farooqui has cited Buxly Paints Bangladesh Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 266. In this case a public company being Buxly Paints (Pakistan) Ltd. became abandoned and vested in the Government by operation of Article 4 of PO 16 of 1972. But before it an agreement had taken place between Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. which was incorporated in erstwhile East Pakistan and which was not abandoned property for acquisition of the interest of the Buxly Paints (Pakistan) Ltd. After the property vested in the Government the Government appointed an administrator to manage the affairs of the company refusing Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. to allow to manage the company in pursuance of the above agreement. This appointment of the Administrator and refusal of the Government to allow the Buxly paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. to manage the affairs of the company was challenged at first by a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution in the High Court Division which rejected the petition and thereafter in the appeal in the Appellate Division of this Court, It was held by the learned Appellate Division of this Court that the Government having stepped into the shoes of Buxly Paints (Pakistan) Ltd. by virtue of the vesting of the property in the Government as abandoned property the Government was under the same obligations as the previous owner was under the contract with the Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. Finding that in part performance of the contract Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. took possession of the Buxly Paints (Pakistan) Ltd, it was also held that by applying section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act the Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd. was entitled to retain its possession against the Government. 

 9. There cannot be any dispute that after the disputed house vested in the Government as abandoned property by operation of Article 4 of PO 16 of 1972 the Government acquired the same right and suffers the same liabilities as the original owner of the disputed house Md. Moinuddin. The deed of agreement shows that possession was delivered by Mr. Moinuddin to the petitioner No. 2 but it is admitted that the petitioner No. 2 left the disputed house in the first week of February, 1972 i.e. before coming into force of PO 16 of 1972 and finding the disputed house vacant the Government entered into possession thereof treating it as abandoned property. In Buxly Paints (Bangladesh) Ltd.'s case the possession of the company was with the petitioner and, as such, the learned Appellate Division of this court held that by applying section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act the petitioner was entitled to retain its possession against the Government in the same way as the petitioner had been entitled to retain against the original owner. In the present case admittedly the petitioners were out of possession on the date on which PO 16 of 1972 came into force. As such, the case cited by Mr. Farooqui cannot be applied to give relief to the petitioner in the present case. 

 10. There is another aspect of the principle that the Government suffers under the same liabilities and enjoys the same right as the original owner Md. Moinuddin, In such case, it has to be decided whether for enforcing a contractual right and which follows from a contract with the original owner Md. Moinuddin the petitioner will be entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction of this Court. The answer is plainly in the negative. Although the Government entered into the house of the previous owner Md. Moinuddin by enforcing a statute, the Government at the same time shoulders the obligations of the contract which the petitioners were entitled to enforce against Md. Moinuddin but this contract is purely a contract of a private nature. The contract between the petitioner No. 1 and the previous owner Md. Moinuddin being purely a private contract was not capable of being enforced in the writ jurisdiction of this Court, As such, since the petitioners seek to enforce the same contract in this writ petition and seek to enforce a right i.e. the right of possession flowing from the said contract of a private nature, it cannot be enforced by this Court in its writ jurisdiction. In this view of the matter also the petitioners cannot get any relief in this writ petition. 

 12. In the result, we find that there is no reason to disturb the decision arrived at by the Court of Settlement and the petitioners are not also entitled to get any relief from this Court in the form of a direction on the respondents to restore possession of the disputed house to them.

parties:
Abdul Jabbar Khan and others  -------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Sreela Sreejukteswar Radha Madhab Thakur Jiew represented by alleged Sebait Sree Kanu Priya Shah Banik and others   -------- Opposite Parties.
