3. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur submits that the plaintiff not having complied with the requirement of Order 7 rule 14 the present petitioners were unable to file written statement controverting the assertions made in the plaint. He submits that the petitioners did not accept the plaintiff as a landlord rather they have taken lease from Bazlur Rahman. Mr. Gafur submits that whether Bazlur Rahman is the owner of the property or not is to be ascertained from the documents of title of the plaintiff as well as original agreement entered into between the landlord and the tenant on inspection of the documents referred to in the plaint. 

 4. Mr. Jagodish Chandra appearing on behalf of Mr. L. Gomee felt difficulty to support the impugned order in view of the requirement of Or. 7, r 15 CPC and in view of the statement made in Annexure B to this petition. Annexure B' is an application seeking inspection of the documents referred to earlier by me. The order impugned has deprived the defendants of their right of inspection of the documents referred to in the plaint which was necessary for filing written-statement. A defendant is entitled to inspection of the documents referred in in the plaint. The order impugned has led to failure of justice.

caseno:
Civil Revision case No. 71 of 1987 
with
Civil Revision case No. 73 of 1987
parties:
Md. Shahabuddin  ----- Petitioners
VS
The Janata Bank Bangladesh represented by the Managing Director & ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The Civil Revision Case No. 71 of 1987 has been heard together with Civil Revision Case No. 73 of 1987 and these two cases are being disposed of by this judgment and order, as substantially similar questions of law and facts are involved therein. Civil Revision Case No. 71 of 1987 has been preferred by petitioner Md. Shahabuddin against the judgment and decree passed by the District Judge, Barisal, in Title Appeal No. 141 of 1986 which arose out of Title Suit No. 810 of 1986 (originally Tiller Suit No. 533 of 1983 of Munsif's 2nd Court, Barisal) of the Munsif's First Court, Barisal. On the other hand, Civil Revision No. 73 of 1987 has been preferred by petitioner A.B.M. Hamid Khan against the judgment and decree passed by the District Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 142 of 1986 which arose out of Title Suit No. 188 of 1985 of the same Munsif's First Court, Barisal. Title Suit No. 533 of 1983 and Title Suit No. ]88 of 1985 were instituted on 27-9- 83 and 18.4.85 respectively. Both the suits were decreed by the learned Munsif by separate judgments on 30.8.86, but the learned District Judge also in separate judgments dated 26.2.87 allowed the appeals and dismissed the suits. 

 3. All the first 4 defendants of both the suits (wrongly described as defendant numbers 2-5 in Title Suit No. 188 of 1985) contested the suits by filing joint written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaints and pleading non-maintainability of the suits in the Civil Court. They contended that the termination of the plaintiffs' services was termination simplicity passed bonafide by competent authority. It was further contended that the plaintiffs being workers as defended in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act their remedy lay in the Labour Court and the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suits. 

 4. In Both the suits the respective plaintiffs alone examined themselves on their behalf and on the other side Mr. Md. Amjad Hossain, Senior Principal Officer, Head Office, Janata Bank deposed as the sole D.W. In Title Suit No. 810 of 1986 the telegram and the plaintiffs termination letter have been marked Exhibit 'E' and Exhibit 3 respectively and in title suit No. 188 of 1985 the plaintiffs termination letter has been marked Exhibit B. Photostat- copies of the relevant noting’s in the Office file together with a list of employees have been marked Exhibit C' and 'D' and Exhibits 'E' and 'F' in the two suits respectively. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record found that the plaintiffs were not workers and as such the suit') were maintainable, the termination order had been issued by incompetent authority and that the orders were punitive in nature. Accordingly he decreed the suits allowing to the plaintiffs the relief prayed for therein together with some additional reliefs directing the defendants to allow the plaintiffs to resume their duties and to pay them their back wages within 30 days. Against the judgments and decrees the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 141 of 1986 and Title Appeal No. 142 of 1986 which have been heard and disposed by the learned District Judge. The learned judge appears to have been silent as to the punitive nature or other- wise of the termination order but has held that the relationship between the parties are governed by the Master and Servant Rule. He has also raised a new question of delegation of authority by the competent authority to the subordinate authority in terminating the plaintiffs' services, and in Title Appeal No. 142 of 1986 has raised a new question as to the proper forum of the suit (Title Suit No. 188 of 1985) being the Administrative Tribunal. According to him the remedy of plaintiff Md. Shahabuddin of the other suit lies in the Labour Court presumably for the reason that the employees of the Bank fall within the definition of the "worker" under the Labour Laws. He has accordingly allowed the appeals and dismissed the suits. The instant Rules have been issued at the instance of the plaintiffs. 

 15. It appears from Exhibits C and D of Title Suit No. 810 of 1986 which are the same as Exhibits E and F of Title Suit No. 188 of 1985 that on 12.9.81 that is one day after the plaintiffs went on strike for indefinite period Mr. Rafiqul Kabir, Assistant General Manager put up a note with lists of concerned employees of different regions including that of Barisal containing the names of the two plaintiffs proposing termination of their services with a further proposal for instruction to the respective Deputy General Manager/Assistant General Manager/ Regional Manager/Branch Manager to issue termination letters. The file was marked to defendant No.2 the Deputy General Manager (Administration) who with his approval placed the file before the General Manager, defendant No.3 who in his turn as noted in his own hand with his signature dated 12.9.81 appears to have discussed the matter with the Managing Director and then accorded his approval to the proposal. It appears that pursuant thereto the Deputy General Manager (Administration) defendant No.2 sent the telegram dated 15.9.81 (EXLE) to defendant No. I who in his turn issued on 17.9.81 the impugned termination letters in the following language:- "This is to inform you that your services in the Bank is terminated with immediate effect. You will be paid salary in lieu of notice period and benefits as admissable. You are requested to collect your salary and other benefits due to you on any working day from the branch/officer where you were serving after adjustment of your liabilities with any bank if any."

parties:
Arun Bhowmick & ors ------ Petitioners.
Vs. 
Salim Reza & ors ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. The petitioner's case, in short, is that one Gopal Chandra Bhowmik instituted Title suit No. 83 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Comilla against one Suruj Miah, the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No.1-15 and others for declaration of right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit properties and also for declaration that the alleged general Power of Attorney dated 15.11.63 alleged to have been executed by the plaintiff and his uncle Khirode Chandra Bhowmik in favour of defendant No. 1 is false, fraudulent, collusive, void, fabricated etc. and also for confirmation of possession of the plaintiff in the suit properties and also for permanent injunction. The, contesting defendant entered appearance and filed written statement on 30.7.84 denying the allegations made in the plaint. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party submits that the learned Munsif while allowing the plaintiffs prayer for recording his evidence on commission failed to appreciate properly and legally, the ground of inability of the plaintiff to appear before the learned Munsif in Court in person. He further argued that excepting the medical certificate nothing has been produced before the learned Munsif in support of the illness of the plaintiff and as this has not been done, the learned Munsif rightly reviewed his earlier order dated 13.9.84. He further submits that the opposite parties were very vigilant and they filed the review petition on 25.9.84 after getting information of the Commission on 23.9.84. They filed this Miscellaneous case at the earliest possible opportunity. He argued that both the Courts below rightly disbelieved the medical certificate as the plaintiff was found present before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Comilla on 9.7.84. He further submits that findings of the District Judge were in full conformity with the provision of rule 7 of Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The District Judge has not arrived at an independent finding but he simply confirmed the finding of the learned Munsif. He further argued that the petitioners are not entitled to any relief in this Rule in view of the concurrent findings of facts by both the Courts below. 

 8. Admittedly, the original plaintiff Gopal Chandra Bhowmik instituted Title Suit No. 83 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif, Comilla against the predecessor-in-interest of opposite parties Nos. 1 to 15 and others. In that suit the plaintiff prayed for declaration of his right, title and interest and confirmation of possession in the suit properties and also prayed for further declaration that the Irrevocable General Power of Attorney dated 15.11.63 alleged to have been executed by the plaintiff and his uncle Gopal Chandra Bhowmik in favour of the defendant No. 1 is false, fraudulent, collusive and fabricated etc. It is also an admitted fact that the plaintiff on 13.9.84 filed a petition supported by a medical certificate with affidavit praying for issuing commission for recording his evidence at his residence on the ground of illness and infirmity. From the persual of the record it is found that the learned Munsif after hearing both the sides allowed the prayer of the plaintiff by his aforesaid order and one Advocate Commissioner was appointed on 16.9.84. It is now the case of the opposite parties that this order dated 13.9.84 was obtained at their back and they filed petition under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for review of this order of appointment of advocate Commissioner for recording his evidence. 

 16. Now let us see whether the opposite party succeeded in placing before the learned Munsif any new and important fact which required him to allow the review petition. It is the definite case of the opposite party in the, petition of review that the petitioner was notseriously ill on the date of filing application for commission before the learned Munsif i.e. on 13.9.84 and hewas in good health to appear before the Court in person and depose. Thepresent petitioners case, is that the original plaintiff was seriously ill and was suffering from Chronic Asthma and bronchitis for the last 2(two) months from the date of issuing of the Medical certificate and he was unable to move and the Deter advised him complete rest. The learned Munsif decided the miscellaneous Case on the basis of the petition for review and the objection filed in this connection. The ground of the review was that the petitioner was not ill. It is the case of the opposite party that the petitioner personal appeared before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Comilla on 9.7.84 in a matter between the same parties and as he appeared before the learned A.D.C. (Rev) on that date it cannot, be found that he was ill during the period mentioned by the Doctor in the Medical Certificate, In paragraph (a) of the petition for review the opposite party stated as follows:- 

 17. This statement of the petitioner in review application clearly indicates and proves t at e predecessor-in-interest of the present petitioners was ill and no other interpretation can be given to these lines mentioned by the opposite party in their petition for review. It also clearly indicates that the opposite parties were fully aware of the illness of the original plaintiff. Under Order 47, rule I of the code of Civil Procedure new and important matter should be brought to the notice of the Court after due diligence which was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him when the order was made. Admittedly the petition for appointing commissioner was made on 13.9.84 and the copy of the same was served upon the lawyer of the opposite party. But no objection was raised by the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party and he never sought any adjournment for giving objection or to get instruction from his client. After the aforesaid statement made in the petition for review on the illness of the plaintiff it cannot be said that the opposite party was not aware of the fact of the illness of the original plaintiff on 13.9.84. This admission on the part of the opposite party in their application for review belied their claim that important fact which was not known to them on 13.9.84 was discovered after due diligence. The person seeking relief under Order 47 rule I should prove certain materials i.e. 'the discovery of new and important matter which 'was not within his knowledge when the order under review' was made and when there is sufficient proof of the matter the review application should be allowed. Here in the present application it cannot be found that the opposite parties were not aware of the illness or otherwise of the original plaintiff on the date when the petition for commission was filed. The learned Advocate for the opposite party relief on certain decisions reported in 38 D.L.R. 47, 35 D.L.R. 461 and A.I.R. 1950(Cal) 178. These decisions were given by Hon'ble Courts in exercise of their revisional power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The facts leading to these decisions are that the Courts below ordered for recording the evidence on commission against which revisional applications were filed and in those revisional applications it was found that in such cases the higher courts had every right to look into the propriety and legality of the order. These decisions were not in connection with the case filed under order 47, rule 1 of the Code and in that view of the matter I hold that the decisions cited by Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate for the opposite party has no manner of application in the present case. The present case arose out of an application filed under Order 47, rule 1 C.P.C. and it must be decided in accordance with the provisions of this law. 

 18. It has been argued by the learned Advocate for opposite patty that opposite parties were not aware of the filing of the petition for commission on 13.9.84 and as such they failed to bring to the notice of the learned Munsif the fact that the original plaintiff was not ill. But from perusal of the record it appears that the learned Advocate appeared on their behalf and contested the matter and if they had any grievances against the order of the learned Munsif they ought to have preferred a revisional application under section 115 c.P.c. But when they preferred to file an application under Order 47, rule I of the Code they must strictly follow this provision. I have already found that the opposite parties themselves admitted that the original plaintiff was ill and in such circumstances there is no ground to disbelieve the petitioners' case. 

 19. Both the Courts below disbelieved the medical certificate issued by the attending physician of the original plaintiff and they held that the original plaintiff was not ill. The medical certificate runs as follows:- 

 20. From the perusal of the medical certificate it is found that on 26.8.84 the Doctor certified that the original plaintiff was under treatment for Bronchitis and Asthma for the last 2 months. The 1stpart of the certificate clearly indicates that the plaintiff-petitioner was suffering for last 2 months prior to 26.8.84. This also indicates that even on the date of issuing certificate the petitioner was ill. In the second part of the certificate the Doctor opined that the original plaintiff was bed ridden and too weak to move and he advised him complete rest in bed and treatment till recovery. The certificate indicates that on 26.8.84 the petitioner was ill and bed ridden. This fact gets support in paragraph 3(a) of the petition for review where the petitioners-opposite parties stated that the original plaintiff was not" so ill" meaning thereby he was ill. The Courts below disbelieved this certificate on the ground that during 2(two) months prior to 26.8.84 the petitioner appeared before A.D.C. (Rev) Comilla on 9.7.84. But mere appearence and giving evidence before the A.D.C. (Rev.) cannot be a ground to dispute the certificate. The latter part of the certificate clearly indicates the physical condition of the original plaintiff. From the perusal of the report of the Advocate commissioner, which is a part of the record it is also found that at the time of recording the evidence on commission the original plaintiff was found seriously ill and admittedly this plaintiff died immediately thereafter. This situation also indicates that the original petitioner was seriously ill and there was nothing to disbelieve the medical certificate. 

 21. In this case while disposing of the review petition the learned Munsif has not specifically found that the petitioners were not aware of the fact that the original plaintiff was not ill or that he was physically fit to appear before the court and he has not found that this new and important fact was brought to the notice of the court after due diligence. From the perusal of the order of the learned Munsif it is found that while disposing of the matter he acted as if sitting as an appellate court and not as original court applying and appreciating the provision of Order 47, rule 1 C.P.C. The learned Munsif sought to have clearly applied that provision of Order 47, rule 1 and come to a definite finding under that provision of law. In that view of the matter I hold that the learned Munsif committed illegality in passing the order dated 29.1.85 and the learned District Judge simply dittoed the finding of the learned Munsif although he was required to come to a definite finding under Order 47, rule 7 of the Code and as such his order passed in appeal cannot also be accepted. 

 23. Though application was filed under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, from the plain reading of that application it is found that the opposite party has not taken any ground that certain new and important facts required for the disposal of the matter in question were not known to them but they after due diligence discovered that fact which are required to be appreciated under the aforesaid provision of the Code. I have gone through the application from which it is found that the opposite party sought to re-open the whole question of appointment of Advocate Commissioner for recording the evidence which law has not provided. The Court has already appointed an Advocate Commissioner and if that order is to be reviewed then the party should. come strictly under the provision of Order 47, rule 1 of the Code and not under any other provision. From a reading of Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure it will be evident that review may be granted only under specific circumstances to meet certain specific situations and not for reopening the order in question on any ground. In the present case the opposite party tried to reopen the matter of appointment of an Advocate Commissioner by way of review without strictly complying with the provision of Order 47, rule 1, C.P.C. In that view of the matter I hold that the opposite parties were not entitled to any relief in the review application. The learned Munsif as well as the learned District Judge failed to appreciate the legal position properly and correctly and they also failed to further appreciate the materials on record particularly the petition for review itself and the medical certificate and as such they committed an error of law which requires interference.

parties:
Jamaluddin ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Rabeya Begum ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
2. A suit for specific performance of an alleged contract was filed by the plaintiff Mosammat Rabeya Begum against defendant No.1 Sree Shankar Karmakar and defendant No.2 since deceased Krishna Rani Karmakar. The Government of Bangladesh was also impleaded as defendant No. 3 in the said suit. It was alleged that the properties originally belonged to one Rama Rani Karmakar who entered into a contract with the plaintiff for sale of the property in question, and executed a bainapatera on 12-7-74 on receipt of an advance of Tk. 15,001. It was agreed that the balance of the consideration will be paid before the execution and registration of the kabala. Rama Rani died on 21-6-76 leaving her heirs defendants 1 and 2 who refused to execute the kabala on 4-8-76. The plaintiff, accordingly, filed the suit for specific performance of the aforesaid contract. Mohammad Shamsul Huq and his wife Mosamaat Hasina Begum claiming to have purchased the property in question from defendant No. 1 alone by a kabala dated 11-9-76 filed an application under Order I, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 4-2-78 for being added as defendant to the suit. It was stated in the petition that during the pendency of the suit, they have purchased the properties, and that as the defendants 1 and 2 have no subsisting interest in the properties they are no longer interested in defending the suit property. 'The learned Sub-ordinate Judge rejected the prayer by the impugned order which runs as follows:— 

 "The necessary parties in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale are the parties to the contract, or if they are dead their legal representatives, as also a person who had purchased the property from the vendor after the contract. He is necessary party as lie would be affected, if he is a volunteer, or if a purchaser for value, had purchased with notice of the contract. A person who claims adversely to the Vendor is however, not a necessary party. Where the property stands in the name of person other then the vender, and the suit for specific performance is brought by the purchaser, that person may be joined as a defendant as a proper party on an allegation that he is the benamidar of the vendor but if he appears and contends that he is not the benamidar of the vendor the proper procedure would be to discharge him from the suit, leaving it to the plaintiff in the suit for specific performance to institute a suit against him after he had got the conveyance in execution of the decree for specific performance against his Vendor. This is on the principle that the scope of a suit for specific performance of a contract also ought not to be enlarged and the suit turned also into a title "Suit between one of either of the parties to the contract and a stranger to the contract." 

 "Specific performance of contract may be enforced under section 27 against either party to the contract or any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract. In view of this provision in section 27 a prior purchaser ought to impaled a subsequent purchaser as a party to the suit for specific performance, because he is a necessary party inasmuch as, by a decree in favour of the prior purchaser the subsequent purchaser's right in the property is effected since if the sale deed executed by the seller in favour of the prior purchaser is registered, it being of a prior date to the sale in favour of the subsequent purchaser, his title to the land will be immediately affected by it." 

 "If the subsequent transferees have taken the property without notice, the consequence, of course, is that the plaintiff's claim cannot succeed; but if they are transferees with notice, as the plaintiff's case is, I do not see why the form should not apply to this case. Specific performance under section 27 of the Specific Relief Act can be claimed against a party to the con-tract as well as any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract." 

 "It cannot be said that in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale or lease a subsequent transferee is not an interested party; for, a subsequent transferee for value, who has paid his money in good faith without notice of the original contract, is entitled to hold his title against the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of the contract. But the objection in the case is that the lease in favour of the petitioner is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, it having been executed during the pendency of a contentious suit. Where a transfer is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, the transferee is not entitled to hold his title against a party to the suit sought to be affected by the transfer. That appears clearly from these words in section 52 of the Transfer of Properly Act, namely; 

 7. Mr Gafur has drawn our attention to a decision of the West Pakistan High Court in the case of Malik Mohammad Ishaque and another vs Mirza Alamos Ali Beg 21 DLR (WP) 333. This decision has no application in the facts of the instant case. The facts are distinguishable. The next case referred to by Mr. Gafur is the case of Momtaj Ali Karim vs. Abul Hossain 22 DLR 146. In this case also the facts are distinguishable and the principle enunciated there cannot be applied to the facts of the instant case. It has been held that in a case for specific performance of contract, conveyance in favour of subsequent transferee is not affected for want of its registration provided the transferee has paid the purchase money in good faith without notice of the original contract. In such case conveyance is not hit by the doctrine of lis pendens though it is registered after the institution of the suit. The Transferee in such case is protected by the exception of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. 

 8. The next case relied upon by Mr. Gafur is that of Fazar Ali vs Abut Kasem Shaikh 22 DLR 240. The facts have no resemblance with the facts of the instant case. The learned Single Judge took the view in the facts of that case alone and the principle cannot be applied in the facts of the instant case. The last case cited by Mr Gufar is the case of Lala Durga Prasad and another vs Lala Deep Chand reported in 1954 SC 934. In this case a subsequent purchaser was impleaded by the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of a contract. The question arose, what should be the form of the decree since the practice of the courts in India was not uniform. It was held that the proper form of the decree was to direct specific performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and direct the subsequent transferee to join the conveyance so as to pass the title, which resides in him to the plaintiff. This principle would have applied if the subsequent transfer was made before the institution of the suit by the plaintiff for specific performance of the contract between plaintiff and his vendor. In such a case the subsequent purchaser will be a necessary party for securing complete title in the event of plaintiff's success in the suit. In the instant case, the subsequent transfer took place during the pendency of the plaintiff's suit for specific performance of the Contract against his vendor. These are all the decisions which Mr. Gafur wished us to consider in support of his contention. 

 9. We do not intend to extend the scope of a suit for specific performance of an alleged contract and to convert it into a suit for title. In our View section 27 of the Specific Relief Act does not contemplate a suit for adjudication of title between a party to contract and a purchaser pcndentelite from one of the parties to the contract. The case of an assignee stands on a completely different footing. Since the transfer was made by defendant No. I during the pendency of the suit, the petitioners are bound by the results of the suit under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Their title if any, is subject to the result of the suit. In such circumstances their presence is neither necessary nor proper for "effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle, all the questions involved in the suit." Further, if does not stand to reason that a volunteer can throw himself on a plaintiff who alone has the right to claim relief for the cause of action against the persons involved. It may be remembered that the provisions of Order I rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure are necessarily subject to the provisions of Order I rules 1 & 2 and Order 2 rule 3 of the said Code. If the plaintiff fails to implead a necessary party he will suffer the consequences. The plaintiff had no cause of action against the present petitioners who claim to purchasers from defendant No. 1 during the pendency of the suit. In our opinion, the petitioners do not come within the category of persons whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to "enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit." The learned Sub-ordinate Judge appears to have judicially exercised his discretion under the provisions of Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. No error in the exercise of jurisdiction by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge could be pointed out by Mr Gafur.
justice_names: Mr. Justice A.R.M. Amirul Islam Chowdhury

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 443 of 1965.
parties:
Abdul Khaleque Sowdagar and another ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Mohammad Fazlul Huq and another ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J - This appeal is at the instance of defendant No.2 against a judgment of reversal decreeing a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession. 

 3. Defendant No. 1 did not appear in the suit but it was contested by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 who filed a joint written statement contenting, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation and was not maintainable in the present form and that it was defendant No.1 who had set up the plaintiff to prosecute the suit on his behalf. The substantive defence case is that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were tenants in respect of the disputed land under one Indra Narayan Datta in 1917 Defendant No. 1 after having acquired the interest of the said Indra Narayan recognized defendant Nos. 2 and 3 as tenants of the disputed land. Thereafter, in 1949 defendant No. 1 contracted to sell the land to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 for and of Rs. 10,000/- out of which Rs. 2,000/- was paid but due to laches on the part of defendant No. 1, there was delay in execution of the promised deed. Thereafter, when in 1957 defendant Nos. 2 and 3 passed upon defendant No. 1 for implementation of the contract in their favour, defendant No. 1 executed a patta for a term of 9 years in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 on 15-4-57 and also a kabala in respect of the rent-receiving interest of the said land in favour of the wives of the said defendants on 15-4-57 and received the balance of consideration money. But defendant No 1 having entered into an unholy alliance with the plaintiff executed a collusive bainanama in his favour and did not register the aforesaid although the patta was duly registered on 15-4-57. In consequence, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were obliged to institute the other Suit No. 23 of 1957 against defendant No. 1 and others for registration of the said kabala. The contesting defendants have been in possession of the disputed land and have constructed huts and building on the said land alter raising its level or business purpose to the knowledge of both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 without any obstruction from any of them and as such the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the said land. 

 4. Upon the aforesaid pleadings certain issues were framed and evidence was led by the parties in respect of their respective contentions. The High court on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record came to the finding that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 had been possessing the disputed land since 1946 as tenants and thereafter as purchasers on the basis of purchase from defendant No. 1 in 1949 and that they been possessing the disputed land since 1949 by virtue of the right acquired by them by making improvements of, and construction on the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge however held that defendant No. 1 had contracted to sell and thereafter sold the land in 1949 to the defendant Nos. 2 and 1 for valuable consideration. On the question whether the patta marked Ext. C. executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant Nos 2 and 3 and the kabala marked Ext. D executed by defendant No.1 in favour of the wives of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 constituted a single transaction amounting to a sale of he disputed land, was placed on of the contesting defendants in the trial court upon the decision reported in Md. Hossain Mia Vs. Member, Board of Revenue, 14 D.L R Dacca. page 87 in which it was held that a deed of lease followed immediately by a deed of sale of the rent-receiving interest of the lease hold property in favour of the same person constituted a transaction of out and our sale of the property But the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have distinguished the said case on the ground that in the instant case the kabala Ext. D was not in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the repents of the Patta, Ext. C but in favour of their and as such was of the opinion that the deed of lease, Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D did not constitute a single transaction of sale, but were two separate transaction. On that view of the matter the deed of lease, Ext C executed by defendant No 1 in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was held to have been hit by section 9 and section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and as such was null and void in the eye of law The learned Subordinate Judge however, held that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acquired good title to the disputed land on the basis of continuous possession of the same for more than 12 years. He came to further findings that defendant No. 1 was in charge of the prosecution of the suit on behalf of the plaintiff and that the bainanama, Ext. 1 purported to be executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiff was a collusive document, the suit was dismissed on the basis of the aforesaid findings. 

 5. The plaintiff preferred an appeal against the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, which being heard by the Court of the Additional District Judge, Chittagong was allowed and the suit was decreed declaring the plaintiff's title to the disputed land and also decreeing recovery for Khas possession of the disputed land by evicting defendant No. 2 and 3 therefrom. In course of the Judgment, the learned Additional District Judge came to the findings that the story of tenancy in respect of the disputed land since 1940 as set up by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was a mere concoction that there was no contract to sell in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in respect of the disputed land in 1949 nor any earnest money was paid in pursuance of the said contract, that the contesting defendants had been in possession of the disputed land since 1956-57 and that the suit being filed in 1961, mere was no acquisition of valid title by adverse possession. As regards the legal effect of the lease Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D the learned Additional District Judge appears to be of the view, concurrently with the learned Subordinate Judge, that the deed of lease Ext C was void in view of section 9 and section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the kabala, Ext. D, by which the rent-receiving interest was purported to have been transferred was also void in inasmuch as no private person could sell the rent-receiving-interest after the 14th April, 1956. 

 6. Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants contends at the outset that the entire judgment of the learned Additional District Judge has been vitiated on account of his failure to formulate any point for determination as required under the provision of Order 41 , rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. According to the learned Advocate, the learned Additional District Judge has failed to grasp the real point in controversy and as such the findings of the trial court have not been considered by the lower appellate court in their correct perspective and as such the said findings have not been properly reversed. The learned Advocate for the appellants has next submitted that both the courts below committed an error of law in failing to construe the deed of lease, Ext, C and kabala, Ext. D correctly and in holding that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 did not acquire any title to the disputed land on the basis of the said documents. Another contention urged on behalf of the appellant is that the finding of possession of the lower appellate court in reversal of the finding given by the trial court in this regard was not proper. The last contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 having acquired valid title on the basis of Exts C and D which would constitute an out and out sale by defendant No 1 in favour of defendant Nos 2 and 3 and other Suit No 9 of 1949 having been decreed only against defendant No. 1 and the relief prayed for in the said suit against defendant Nos. 2 and 3 having been refused, the title acquired by defendant Nos. and 3 on the basis of Exts. C and D would prevail over any title which may be claimed by the plaintiff on the basis any instrument purported to be executed on behalf of the defendant No.1 after the aforesaid deeds executed in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3. 

 8. As regards the contention on the question of possession we do not think that the finding which has been arrived at by the lower appellate court reversing the finding of the trial court in this regard can he interfered with in the second appeal. The learned Advocate for the appellant has not been able to point out any material piece of evidence which was considered by the trial court in arriving at the finding that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 have been in possession for more than 12 years of the disputed land on assertion of their title by purchase of the said land, but has not been adverted to by the lower appellate court while it reversed the aforesaid finding. The contesting defendants' case is that the said defendants has been in possession of the disputed land since 1946 as tenants under one Indra Narayan Datta whose interest was subsequently purchased by defendant No.1 in a money sale. The learned Additional District Judge has observed that not a scrap of paper has been produced by the defendants to show that the defendants were tenants under the Datta's or that defendant No. 1 ever accepted any rent from defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and have granted a receipt for the same. It has also been pointed out that the recitals in Ext.C the deed of lease executed on the 12th of April 1957 on the basis of which defendant Nos. 2 and 3 claimed their title, show that they have been possessing the house on the disputed land as ‘monthly bharatia’ under the Datta's and after them under defendant No. 1. The learned Subordinate Judge has of course construed the word ‘bharatia’ as the tenant in respect of the land. The learned Additional District Judge has however differed from the learned Subordinate Judge on this point. Nothing has been placed before us to show that the view taken by the learned Additional District Judge in this regard was not correct to any view of the matter it seems to us that defendant Nos. 1 and 3 accepted defendant No. 1 as the real owner in possession on the basis of the deed of lease and the kabala executed by dfdt. No 1. It cannot he said that defendant Nos. 2and 3 exercised any right in respect of the disputed land adverse to that of defendant No.1 prior to the said deed. The date of the commencement of the adverse possession of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 cannot in any view be pushed further back from the date of the execution of the said documents. The case of the contesting defendants will have to be established, if at all, on the basis of the title purported to have been acquired on the basis of the documents, Exts.C and D and not on the basis of adverse possession. 

 9. So it appears to us that the main question in this appeal is whether the documents, Exts C and D together constitute a valid transaction of an out and out sale and whether they will be of any value to defendant Nos 2 and 3 for establishing their title as against the plaintiff in view of the Decree passed in other Suit No. 9 of 1959. 

 “If a transaction is entered into by more than one document, both the documents should, in our opinion be read together and their combined effect considered. In the present case the intention of the parties was clearly to affect an out and out transfer of all the right, title and interest of the transferor to the transferee. How this could be affected conveniently, whether by one document or by more than one document, was not very material. What had to be ascertained upon a proper consideration of these two documents together was as to what was the intention of the parties. If the intention was to make a complete out and out transfer, then the transaction was a sale and not merely a lease, even though it may have been camouflaged as a lease for 99 years coupled with a conveyance of the residuary rent receiving interest absolutely which together effected a transfer of the entire bundle of rights of the transferor in these lands." 

 13. We have, therefore, no hesitation in ho ding that these two documents together constitute one and single transaction of out and oat sale and bosh the courts how committed an error of law in construing the said and in considering the said transaction essentially to be a lease which being hit by sections 9 and 75A of the East Bengal state Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was null and void In the said event defendant Nos 2 and 3 acquired good title in the disputed land by purchase on 15-4-57. 

 14. Now the question remains whether the said title of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 has been affected in any way by the decree which the plaintiff obtained in other suit No.9 of 1959 as well as by the kabala executed and registered through court in pursuance of the decree passed in the said suit. The plaintiff brought the aforesaid suit against the defendant Nos. 1-3 for specific performance of contract evidenced by the bainanama, Ext. 1 dated 5-11-56. The title acquired by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by virtue of Exts. C and D having arisen subsequent to the aforesaid bainanama, the plaintiff could have enforced the agreement for sale against defendant Nos. 2 and 3 provided he could establish that defendant Nos. and 3 were not transferees’ for value or did not pay their money in good faith or that they had notice of the prior contract for sale. At the moment when the said suit was brought i.e. on 11-2-59 defendant No 1 had no subsisting interest in the disputed land and any enforcement of the contract dated 15-11-56 against him alone and executive and registration of kabala Court on his behalf would not create any title in respect of the disputed land in favour of the plaintiff, and therefore, the plaintiff rightly impleaded the said defendant Nos. 2 and 3 along with defendant No. 1 for specific performance of contract as is contemplated in section 27 of the Specific Relief Act although he did not properly appreciate the real nature of the transaction. The plaintiff took the transaction evidenced by Exts. C & D to be a lease and prayed for cancellation of the said lease in the suit. The suit for specific performance of contract was decreed against defendant No. 1 but the prayer for cancellation of the lease was rejected by the court on the view that the said prayer for cancellation of the lease was not within the scope of that suit. The learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have been quite correct in refusing to consider the question of validity of the subsequent lease as against the plaintiffs' claim for specific performance of the contract on the ground that it was beyond the scope of that suit. 

 15. There appears to have been some conflict of judicial views regarding the form of the decree which may be passed in a suit of specific performance of contract against the original contracting party and his transferee. Mr. Mozammel Huq the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant has placed before us the case of Kafiluddin and others Vs Saminuddin and others reported in A.I.R 1931 Cal. 67 same case 34 C.W.N. 698 in which a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court observed as follows: 

 "It would appear that the procedure adopted in passing decrees in such case is not uniform but it is proper that the English procedure supported by the Specific Relief Act should be adopted. The apparent reasoning is that unless both the contracting parties and the subsequent purchaser join in the conveyance it is possible that difficulties may arise with regard to the Plaintiff's title. Suppose in a case in which the contracting party did not appear and the decree passed directed the sub sequent purchaser only to convey the property to the plaintiff. The original vendor may subsequently raise the objection that his title had not passed for want of consideration or otherwise to the subsequent purchaser and therefore the conveyance executed by the subsequent our chaser in favour of the plaintiff did not pass good title. In order to avoid all controversies of this sort that may be available it is proper that conveyance should he executed in favour of the plaintiffs in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale by the contracting party as well as by the subsequent transferee of his interest" 

 "When a person with knowledge of a previous contract of sale purchases the property the purchase is at the option of the prior promise and the contract with him can be enforced specifically against the subsequent purchaser. In such a suit the court should declare the second purchase as null and void and cancel it and order the original promisor to carry out his contract by executing the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff." 

 17. The form of decree which should be adopted in framing a decree for specific performance of contract came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of India in the case of Durga Prasad Vs. Deep Chand reported in A.I.R 1954 SC 75. The aforementioned cases of the Calcutta and Allahabad High Court were considered by the Supreme Court of India in the said case and it was noticed that the practice of the court in India had not been uniform and three distinct lines of thought emerged. According to one point of view the proper form of decree was to declare the subsequent purchase void as against the plaintiff and contract was to be conveyance by the vendor alone. According to the second point of view, both the vendor and the vendee should join while the third view would limit the execution of the conveyance to the subsequent purchaser alone. In discussing the corporative merits of these various forms of decrees which may be passed in a suit for specific performance of contract against the original contracting party and subsequent transfer the view of the Supreme Court of India was expressed in the said decision in the following manner. 

 "First, we reach the position that the title to the property has validity passed from the vendor and resides in the subsequent transferee. The sale to him not void but only voidable at the option of the earlier 'contractor' As the title no longer rests in the vendor it would be illogical from a conveyancing point of view to compel him to convey to the plaintiff unless steps are taken to re-vest the title in him either by cancellation of the subsequent sale or by re-conveyance from, the subsequent purchaser to him. We do not know of any case in which a re-conveyance to the vendor was ordered but Sulaiman, C. J. adopted the other course in Kali Charan Vs. Janak Deo, A.I.R. 1932 All. 694. He directed the cancellation of the subsequent sale and conveyance to the plaintiff by the vendor in accordance with the contract of sale of which the plaintiff sought specific performance. But though this sounds logical the objection to it is that it might bring in its train complications between the vendor and the subsequent purchaser we are not enamored of the next alternative either, namely conveyance by the subsequent purchaser alone to the plaintiff. It is true that would have the effect of vesting the title to the property in the plaintiff but it might be inequitable to compel the subsequent transferee to enter into terms and covenants in the vendor's agreement with the plaintiff to which he would never have agreed had he been a free agent………….. In our opinion the proper form of decree is to direct the specific performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and direct the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance so as to pass on the title which resides in him to the plaintiff. He does not join in any special covenants made between the plaintiff and his vendor; all he does is to pass on his title to the plaintiff. This was the course followed by the Calcutta High Court in Kafiluddin Vs Samiuddin". 

 From a consideration of the view expressed in the aforesaid decision of the Supreme Court of India it is clear that mere obtaining a decree for specific performance of contact against the original contracting party after he has transferred his interest to another person and procuring kabala through court on behalf of the said contracting party cannot affect the interest of the subsequent transferee in any way because the transfer in his favour was not void but merely voidable at the option of the promise of the original contract under certain circumstances. If by the decree of the court the transfer in his favour is not declared null and void or cancelled nor he is compelled to convey his interest which be acquired by subsequent purchase, the promise does not acquire any title in the disputed property by virtue of the decree or the kabala he may hate obtained against or from the original contracting party. Relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court of India, Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate for the appellant contended that the title acquired by the defendant No. 2 on the basis of Exts. C and D have not been affected in any way by the decree which was obtained by the plaintiff in the earlier suit for specific performance of contract against defendant No. 1 and as such there is no base for the plaintiff's claim of title. We find substance in this contention of the learned Advocate. In the suit for specific performance of contract, the transfer in favour of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 effected by means of Exts. C and D have not been declared void or cancelled nor they having been compelled to join in the conveyance executed and registered through court on behalf of defendant No. 1 who had no subsisting interest in the disputed land at that time in the disputed property. The plaintiff did not acquire any title to the said property which had been vested in defendant Nos. 2 and 3 before the said suit was instituted. It is unfortunate that the plaintiff finds himself in such a situation on account of misconception of the legal position in this regard. 

 However we cannot, but accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant on this point. In that view of the mater, we are of the opinion that the plaintiff has failed to establish his title in respect of the disputed land.

parties:
Mrs. Afsana Barik Malik. ------- Defendant No.2-petitioner.
Vs.
Zakaria Hossain Chowdhury and others ------- Plaintiff-opposite parties.
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 09.01.2022 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 570 of 2018 rejecting the petitioner’s application under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The brief fact relevant for disposal of this Rule is that the opposite party No.1, Zakaria Hossain Chowdhury as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 570 of 2018 in the Court of the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka praying the following reliefs: 

 a) Pass a decree that the Plaintiff has title to the 1,00,000 shares (originally 10,000 shares of BDT 100 each that were converted to 1,00,000 shares of BDT 10 each as per Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission's order No. SEC/CMRRCD/2009-193/109 dated 15.09.2011) registered in the name of the defendant No.2 and 1,00,000 shares (originally shares of BDT 100 each that were converted to 1,00,000 shares of BDT 10 each as per Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission's Order No. SEC/CMRRCD/2009-193/109 dated 15.09.2011) registered in the name of Mrs. Roksana Islam (the predecessor of Defendant Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) in the share registered of Defendant No.1 Bank and any right shares, bonus shares and dividend arising there from calculated from the date of the agreement for Amicable Partition dated 25.06.1999 till date; 

 b) Pass a decree directing the Defendant No.1 Bank of rectify its share register and insert the name of the Plaintiff in the place of Defendant No.2 and Mrs. Ruksana Islam (predecessor of Defendant Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) in connection with the 1,00,000 shares (originally 10,000 shares of BDT 100 each that were converted to 1,00,000 shares of BDT 10 each as per Bangladesh securities and Exchange Commission's Order No. SEC/CMRRCD/2009-193/109 dated 15.09.2011 registered in the name of the Defendant no.2 and 1,00,000 shares (originally 10,000 shares of BDT 100 each that were converted to 1,00,000 shares of BDT 10 each as per Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission's Order No. SEC/CMRRCD/2009-193/109 dated 15.09.2011) registered in the name of Mrs. Roksana Islam (The predecessor of Defendant Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) and any right shares, bonus shares and divided arising therefore calculated from the date of the Agreement for Amicable Partition dated 24.06.1999 till date; 

 d) Award such other or further relief or reliefs as the plaintiff may be entitled to in law and equity. 

 4. In this backdrop, while the suit was in progress the defendants filed an application under Order VII, Rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint stating, interalia, that the contents of the plaint do not disclose any cause of action of the suit, the suit is barred by limitation, the plaintiff earlier over the self-same subject matter filed Title Suit No. 420 of 2004 for declaration of title and thereafter having realized the difficulties the plaintiff filed an application for withdrawal of the suit with a permission to sue afresh which was allowed on 02.10.2005 and thereafter, the plaintiff long lapses of 14 years over the self-same subject matter filed the present suit praying similar type of reliefs which is clearly barred by the principle of res-judicature, the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as daylight such a suit should be buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation. The subject matter of the instant suit is clearly and completely company matter and a case being Company Matter No. 112 of 2005 had filed by the present plaintiff which was also disallowed by judgment and order dated 31.05.2018 passed by a Company Bench of this Court and as such, at any rate the plaint of the suit is liable to be rejected to secure the ends of justice. 

 "But so far the allegation as has been brought in the instant application that the respondent No. 1 company has unlawfully denied to register the transfer of the shares so far it concerns to the respondent Nos. 3 and 5, the same has got no merit on the ground that the allegedly submitted from 117 to the respondent No. 6 Bank were inadequate and submission of original share certificates along with non-executed form 117, cannot constitute a valid transfer of shares. But so far the question as to the entitlement of the petitioner to the said shares owned by the respondent Nos. 2 and 4 is concerned, it appears that the respondent No 2 and 4 have already made compromise with the petitioner and accordingly their shares have already been treated as transferred to the petitioner by way of the compromise effected from the date of compromise.” 

 10. Finally, Mr. A.K. Rashedul Huq submits that the present suit is based on a family settlement which was reduced into writing and duly registered on 24.06.1999 under the title of Family Settlement Agreement; there is a good number of documentary evidences which can be substantiated by the oral evidences during trial in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No.1. The plaintiff also has money receipts and family settlement agreement to prove his case and thus it can safely be said that the suit is not a fruitless litigation. 

 12. Firstly, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner argues that the suit is barred by limitation, in the facts and circumstances of the case the plaintiff is not entitled to get benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act as the suit is clearly time barred being the long gap of more than 14 years. 

 13. It is true that section 14 of the Limitation Act contain the provision to extension of the period of limitation. In this case we have already indicated that the plaintiff earlier filed Title Suit No. 420 of 2004 before the Assistant Judge, Dhaka and thereafter they filed an application to withdraw the suit with liberty to sue afresh and the said application was allowed and soon thereafter, the plaintiff filed Company matter before the Company Bench of this Court being Company Matter No. 112 of 2005 and after hearing of both the sides the company bench disallowed the Company Matter No. 112 of 2005 by its judgment dated 31.05.2018 with a direction that “the disputed question of title to the properties involved in the said issue and as such the question of part performance by the parties under the Family Settlement Agreement dated 24.6.1999 is required to be considered upon evidence in a properly constituted suit for specific performance of contract." And, soon thereafter finding no other way the present plaintiff-opposite party filed the instant Title Suit No. 570 of 2018 impleading the defendant petitioner and others praying the reliefs as quoted above. 

 16. To meet this branch of argument, we have carefully studied the contents of the plaint to the best of our ability and it appears to us that the contents of the plaint do disclose the cause of action for the suit. Moreover, in this case the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 argues that the plaintiff filed the suit based on a family settlement which was reduced into writing and duly registered on 24.06.1999 under the title of Family Settlement Agreement. There are good number of documentary evidences which can be substantiated by the oral evidences during trial in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No.1, the plaintiff also has money receipts and family settlement agreement to prove his case. Therefore, in the above facts and circumstances of the case, we are unable to see eye to eye to such submission of the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner that the suit is a fruitless litigation and the contents of the plaint do not disclose any cause of action for the suit. 

 18. It is true that the subject matter of the case is more or less company bench matter and accordingly, the plaintiff as applicant earlier filed a company matter being No. 112 of 2005 before a appropriate company bench of this Court which was disallowed by judgment and order dated 31.05.2018 with observation that- “But so far the question of entitlement of the petitioner to the transfer of shares held in the name of the respondent Nos. 3 and 5 are concerned, it appears that the disputed question of title to the property is involved in the said issue and as such the question of part performance by the parties under the Family Settlement Agreement dated 24.06.1999 is required to be considered upon evidence in a properly constituted suit for specific performance of contract”

lawyer:
