parties:
Md Abdur Rajjak ------- Appellant
Vs.
Abdul Haye died leaving behind his heirs: I (a) Md. Shahjahan Ali (Shahin) and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The appellant as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 170 of 1967 (which was renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 247 of 1982) for declaration of title and permanent injunction, stating, inter alia, that the suit property originally belonged to East Bengal Mercantile Bank, whose head office was situated in Calcutta and two branch offices were located in Mymensingh and Jamalpur of the then East Pakistan. The said Bank wound up during erstwhile East Pakistan. The Bank was an assessee of Agricultural Income Tax under the Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1944. The suit property was put to auction sale for non-payment of arrear income tax through Certificate Case Nos. 164 AIT/54-55, 165 AIT/55-556 on 10.06.1956 after due service of notice upon the directors of that Bank. The notice of proclamation to the auction sale of the suit property also was duly served upon the directors of the said Bank. The auction sale took place in presence of the Bank officials as well as the defendants Dr. Kudrat Ali and others. The predecessor of the appellant, namely, Mansur Ali participated in that auction sale and whose bid was accepted as the highest one by the concerned certificate officer conducting that auction sale proceeding. 

 5. The appellant as defendant contested that suit stating that the said Amalnama and rent receipt were false, collusive and manufactured in collusion with the Bank officials taking advantage of the deplorable financial plight of the Bank at that period being on the verge of liquidation. That Dr. Kudrat Ali with the help of the defendant No. 2 wrongfully entered into illegal possession of the suit land and continued there till dispossession by the certificate officer for inducting auction purchaser Mansur Ali into possession on 21.03.1960. The suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act filed by Dr. Kudrat Ali was dismissed by the learned Trial Court. Dr. Kudrat Ali then preferred- a title appeal before the East Pakistan High Court against the judgment and decree of the Trial Court which was allowed and the suit was decreed. Mansur Ali then preferred a 2nd appeal against the judgment and decree of the High Court before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal with observation that induction of Mansur Ali into possession of the suit property was not in accordance with law. In that appeal the Supreme Court did not discuss about right, title and interest of the plaintiff and the defendant in the suit property and as such the right and ownership was left undecided and hence the plaintiff, in order to seek appropriate relief against the defendant, has filed the suit. 

 6. The respondent-defendant No. 1 con-tested the suit by filling written statement, stating, that, the banking business of East Bengal Mercantile Bank, Jamalpur wound up and the Bank leased out the entire suit property to defendant No. 1 Dr. Kudrat Ali-who firstly took settlement of 20 decimals of C.S. Plot No. 2058 under Khatian No. 255 at a yearly rental of Tk. 65 from Surandra Chowdhury, a director of the said Bank. Thereafter, the defendant No. 1 purchased 4 tin shed huts of that premises from the above director on 22nd Basaikh, 1358 B.S. at an amount of Tk. 400/-. After that defendant No.1 took settlement of another 20 decimals of land including the building thereon at a rental of Tk. 65 per annum through an Amalnama on 28th Baisakh, 1358 B.S. from the above director of the Bank. Since then the defendant No. 1 had possessed the suit property by exercising his own right, title and interest thereon and thus acquired good title by adverse possession also. 

 7. Further case of the defendant No. 1 was that the defendant No. 1 was a doctor who held a dispensary in a room of the suit building. The defendant No. 1 himself also erected two small tin shed huts in the suit land and leased out the same to the tenants who installed a betel shop and a cycle mending shop at a monthly rental shop. The contesting defendant No. 1 has also pleaded that the East Bengal Mercantile Bank was not an agriculturist and no agriculture income tax was imposed upon it. The plaintiff collusively filed a certificate case against the Bank in complicity with the certificate officer with a malafide intention to grab the suit property. No notice was served upon the certificate debtors in accordance with law. Moreover, sale proclamation and the sale certificate were confined to selling the buildings and doors and windows of the buildings on the suit land and that the land was not advertised for sale in the proclamation of sale. That the plaintiff purchased the buildings and doors and windows of the buildings in that auction, that the certificate officer being gained over by the plaintiff ousted the defendant No. 1 and his family from the suit property by illegal force and as such the defendant No. 1 filed Other Class Suit No. 17 of 1961 under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in the 4th Court of the Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh for restoration of possession of the suit building and land measuring 12 decimals out of the suit property and the said suit was decreed upto the Supreme Court. The defendant No. 1 filed the Execution Case No. 4 of 1961 for execution of the said decree. The plaintiff has filed the instant suit to delay of the said execution case. The defendant No. 1 was a tenant under East Bengal Mercantile Bank and he became owner of the suit property after acquisition of the rent receiving interest under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. That the plaintiff did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land by his alleged purchase of the same in auction. The suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 14. He further submits that the Appellate Court below as the last court of fact having held on consideration of the evidence on record that "it can be safely concluded that enormous materials are there on record to substantiate the claim of lawful title, right and interest of the plaintiff on the strength of their auction purchase" the High Court Division erred in ignoring the said finding of fact of the untenable view that by the auction purchase the appellant purchased the schedule property, that is, the building of the Bank and 13 Nos. of windows and 10 pair of doors, and this has resulted in an error in the decision of the case causing grave failure of justice. 

 15. He lastly submits that the High Court Division dismissed the suit without adverting to the findings of fact by the Appellate Court below in any manner and/or reversing the same on the untenable view that "the learned judge of the appellate court failed to consider that plaintiff's title cannot go beyond the land which he purchased in auction" and this has caused grave failure of justice in the case, hence, the instant appeal should be allowed. 

 16. Mr. Subrata Chowdhury, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that as the specific case of the appellant is that his predecessor purchased the suit property through the auction sale which is the basis of his title but in the auction proclamation [Exhibit-3], the schedule described as below: 

 and that the Trial Court after scrutinizing the certified copy of the `Boynama' (Exhibit-1), correctly found that no land was specifically mentioned in the afore-said sale certificate and accordingly held that the appellant did not acquire any title in the suit land and that the High Court Division also considered the aforesaid Exhibit-1 and came to a finding that the plaintiff acquired no title in the suit land by way of the aforesaid auction purchase and the Court of Appeal below, while reversing the judgment of the Trial Court, did not reverse the aforesaid finding of the Trial Court and as such the present appeal is liable to be dismissed in the interest of justice. 

 and accordingly, the Trial Court and as well as the High Court Division rightly found that the plaintiff did not acquire any tile in the suit land by way of the aforesaid auction and that the Court of Appeal below most erroneously held that the plaintiff acquire title by dint of the auction and as such the present civil appeal is liable to be dismissed in the interest of justice. 

 and that according to the aforesaid Boynama Md. Monsur Ali (plaintiff)was the highest bidder in respect of the schedule property which has been described in the schedule of the Boynama and also in the proclamation of the auction and he acquired no title in the suit land as no description or quantum of land was given in Exhibit Nos. 1 and 3 and thus the Trial Court and the High Court rightly dismissed the suit and therefore the present civil appeal is liable to be dismissed by the Appellate Division in the interest of justice. 

 20. He next submits that the present appellant as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No.76 of 2012 before the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Jamalpur (on transfer to the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Bakshganj, Jamalpur, the aforesaid suit was renumbered as Other Class Suit No.218 of 2022) against present respondent Nos.2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 and the predecessors of respondent No.1 and that the aforesaid suit was dismissed for default on 31.10.2022 and that the aforesaid suit was filed praying for a declaration that the ROR and BRS record of the suit land was wrong and the defendant acquires no title by dint of aforesaid records and that it is to be noted that the suit land of Other Class Suit No.170 of 1967 and Other Class Suit No.76 of 2012 are the same and that the legal implication of dismissal of Other Class Suit No.76 of 2012 is that the plaintiff of the aforesaid is debarred from challenging the ROR and BRS record and also the title of the respondents and as such the present civil appeal is liable to be dismissed in the interest of justice. 

 II. For that the Appellate Court as the last court of fact having held on consideration of the evidence on record that "it can be safely concluded that enormous materials are there on record to substantiate the claim of lawful title, right and interest of the plaintiff on the strength of their auction purchase" the High Court Division erred in ignoring the said finding of fact of the untenable view that by the auction purchase the plain-tiff purchased the schedule property, that is, the building of the Bank and 13 Nos. of windows and 10 pair of doors, and this has resulted in an error in the decision of the case causing grave failure of justice. 

 III. For that the High Court Division dismissed the suit without in any manner adverting to the findings of fact by the appellate court and/or reversing the same on the untenable view that "the learned judge of the appellate court failed to consider that plaintiff title cannot go beyond the land which he purchased in auction" and this has caused grave failure of justice in the case.' 

 "..it is by now a well settled legal principle that the finding in a suit for permanent injunction cannot be binding in a suit for title." 

 25. The instant suit is a suit for title, as such, whatever may the findings of Other Class Suit No. 17 of 1961, these are no longer applicable in this case as that case was filed under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1887. 

 26. In a civil suit, the rule for proving any fact/document is the preponderance of evidence, which means the court is to weigh up evidences of both parties and the party whose evidence weighs more will win the case. In the instant case both of the Trial Court and the Appellate Court below concurrently finds that the present respondents failed to establish their title over the suit land. No so called `Amalnama', which was the sole basis of the respondents claimed title over the suit land, was produced before the Trial Court. It reduced their claim of ownership over the suit land to a purely imaginary and aerial claim. As such, the status of the Respondents over the suit land would at best be a usurper only. 

 27. On the other hand, the documentary as well as oral evidences of the plaintiff-appellant herein, were thoroughly examined and some decisions were reduced in writing as judgment. The Appellate Court below, which is the final court of facts, decided that the Appellant was able to establish his right, title and interest over the suit land. However, without reverting these findings, the High Court Division on revisional jurisdiction cannot alter findings of last court of facts. 

 29. Consequently, we too don't find any reason interfere with the concurrent findings of facts regarding lacking of title of the respondents in the suit land. As such, our conscientious view is that High Court Division made an error in the decision of the case causing grave failure of justice. 

 30. Now only question left to be decided by us is whether the concerned auction sale/purchase, Boynama and putting the predecessor of the present appellant in possession by the government officials vests right, title and interest to him over the suit land. 

 31. This question was vividly examined by the Appellate Court and in our opinion it is merit worthy. We too concur with the explanation of the Appellate Court as to that if the auction would only stipulate to the sale of the building along with the doors and windows, the certificate officer would not induct the predecessor of the Appellant into the suit land. The suit land was confiscated in favour of the State for fiscal arrears. This means, title of the suit land transmitted to the State from the title holder East Bengal Mercantile Bank. It is worthy to be mentioned here that title of the East Bengal Mercantile Bank over the suit land is an admitted fact. Therefore, any objection concerning the title of the predecessor of the Appellant over the suit land could only be raised by the Government. In this case, it is crystal clearly evident that Government itself not only sold the suit land to the Appellant but also installed him as the possessor. As such, we opine that the Government waived and acquiesced the title of the suit land over the Appellant and consequently, estopped as well concerning the same issue. If there's any mistake or fault in the total auction sale process and documents that could affect title of the Appellant over the suit land that has also been cured by the Government, through the above mentioned process of waiving and acquisition.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Md. Abu Zafor Siddique

parties:
Elias Ali (Md) -------  Petitioner
VS
Md. Abul Kashem Nur Alam (Mintu) and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioner filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land stating that the suit land originally belonged to one Angari Mondol, CS Khatian No. 21, Plot No. 1177 measuring 1.20 acres and Plot No. 1108 measuring 1.00 acres totalling 2.20 acres of land stands recorded in his name. Angari Mondal died leaving behind two sons namely Rajob Ali Mondal and Monser Ali Mondal and two daughters namely Sutimon Nessa and Asimon Nessa as his legal heirs. At the time of SA record, one Uzir Ali fraudulently got his name recorded in SA Khatian No. 18. The heirs of Angari Mondal upon coming to know the matter filed Title Suit No. 176 of 1967 in the Munsif Court, Dinajpur Sadar and obtained a decree of title in respect of the suit land. Accordingly, SA khatian was corrected vide Case No. 219/27/83-84 and 13/03/90-91 and a new record being Khatian No. 18/1 was prepared in the name of the heirs of said Angari Mondal. By a deed of amicable partition, the suit properties fell in the share of Monser Ali who had been possessing the same exclusively. Monser Ali Mondal died leaving wife Amisa Bewa, one son Elias Ali and three daughters Saleha Khatun, Akjahan Bibi and Banesa Bibi as his heirs. The plaintiff-petitioner got the suit land in his share by a compromise agreement with his sisters and since then, he has been possessing the land by cultivating the same. On 30-8-2006, the defendant No. 1 claimed title to the suit land and hence, the petitioner filed the instant suit. Subsequently, the defendant No. 21 has been added who had purchased the suit land measuring 1.271/2 acres of land from defendants on different dates. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 filed written statement supporting the case of the plaintiff. Added defendant No. 21 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material facts stated in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Angari Mondol which was recorded in his name in CS Khatian No. 21. Angari Mondol died leaving behind two sons Rajob Ali Mondol and Monser Ali Mondol and two daughters Sutimon Nessa and Asimon Nessa as his legal heirs. Thereafter, Khatian No. 18/1 was prepared in the name of the heirs of Angari Mondal. Rajob Ali Mondal died leaving behind three sons namely Iqbal, Aslam and Md. Islam and four daughters namely Kajeman Bibi, Mahila Begum, Aklima and Afroza Bewa i.e. Proforma defendant Nos. 2-8 as his heirs. Monser Ali Mondal died leaving behind his wife Amisa Bewa, one son Elias Ali and three daughters Saleha Begum, Akjahan Bibi and Banesa Bibi, Proforma defendant Nos. 9-12 as his heirs. Sutimon Nessa alias Putli, daughter of Angari Mondal died leaving behind her husband namely Alimuddin, one son Mozahar Ali and daughter Mirjan Bibi, proforma defendant Nos. 13-14 in suit. Asimon Nessa, daughter of Angari Mondal died leaving son Md. Kalam and two daughters Pochimon Nessa and Hazra Bewa, Proforma defendant Nos. 15-17. 

 8. He submits that the suit was filed in fact against the defendant No. 1 who had no connection with the suit property as he is not a co-sharer by inheritance. Other co-sharer have been made as pro-forma defendants. When the suit was proceeding towards hearing, all of a sudden defendant No. 21 came into scene and claimed title in the suit property by purchase during pendency of the suit and got him added as defendant No. 21. 

 9. He submits that evidences led by the plaintiff established that none of the pro-forma defendants were in possession of the suit property and they never raised claim in the suit land, but the defendant No. 21 with mala fide intention somehow managed to create some sale deeds from some of the pro-forma defendants who had no title and possession in the property. The defendant No. 21 got no possession of the property alleged to have been purchased by him on the basis of a bainanama allegedly executed on 5-6-2005, which has been created by the defendant No. 21 on the stamp purchased in the name of one Md. Iqbal Hossain who is neither executant nor purchaser. The trial court rightly held that the bainanama has been created by erasing signature of some person on the stamp paper. 

 10. He also argued that had it been executed by the vendor of the defendant No. 21, it would have been mentioned in the recital of the sale deed, but nothing stated in the deed about execution of any bainanama by the vendor. The trial court also observed that in the event of transfer of property by any of the defendants in suit during pendency is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, and unless the defendant No. 21 can establish title from pro-forma defendants by purchase in an independent suit, the deeds in question cannot create any title in favour of the defendant. 

 11. He finally argued that the defendant as per his deed of sale purchased the property from SA Khatian No. 702, but in the instant case the plaintiff claimed the properties under CS Khatia No. 21 and corrected khatian No. 18/1. The trial court upon consideration of evidences both oral and documentary found exclusive possession of the plaintiff in the suit property and also observed that nothing has come out on cross from the PWs. Moreover, pro-forma defendant Nos. 3 and 4 co-sharers of the plaintiff admitted that the plaintiff acquired right, title and possession in the suit property exclusively by amicable arrangement among all the co-sharers, but the appellate court while allowing the appeal and remanding the suit to the trial court for fresh trial wrongly observed that the dispute between the parties is whether the plaintiff's father acquired title exclusively in the suit property by amicable arrangement among the co-sharers and whether he got exclusive possession of the property completely ousting other co-sharers from the suit land and by that act whether the plaintiff acquired any title in the property without bringing a suit for partition. Where co-sharer defendant Nos. 3 and 4 supported the case of the plaintiff by filing written statement, that father of the plaintiff got the suit property amicably of his share and after his death all the heirs inherited the same and among the plaintiff also absolutely got the property in his share by amicable arrangement among them, there is no need for bringing any suit for partition unless the co-sharer in the property could prove their possession in any portion of the land. In the instant case none of the co-sharer defendants came forward by filing written statement to claim that there was no amicable partition and they are in possession as co-sharer. In the absence of such claim of the co-sharer defendants, the appellate court ought not to have allowed the appeal and sent the case back to the trial court on remand for fresh trial. As such, the appellate court has committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 12. Mr. Ehsan A Siddiq with Mr. Imran A Siddiq, Mr. Chowdhury Ishrak, Ahmed Siddiky, Mr. Mohammad Shahnewaz and Ms. Shadia Afrin Jeny, learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party No. 1 submit that the plaintiff categorically stated that the property originally belonged to one Angari Mondal who died leaving two sons and two daughters who inherited the property. The plaintiff is one of the heirs of Monser Ali Mondal. After the death of Monser Ali plaintiff and his mother and three sisters inherited the property and claimed that by amicable partition among the heirs of Monser Ali he exclusively got the property in his share. The defendants did not deny the share of Monser Ali Mondal inherited from Angari Mondal, but the defendant No. 21 claimed that the plaintiff failed to show any evidence either oral or documentary that Monser Ali Mondal got the property by amicable partition or after his death Elias Ali also got the property in his share by any deed or any evidence. In the absence of any written instrument as admitted by the plaintiff all the heirs of Angari Mondal are co-sharer in the property. Possession of a co-sharer in the property, does not mean that he is owner of the property of other co-sharers, but according to law a co-sharer in possession means that he has been possessing the property for and on behalf of other co-sharers, unless he could prove that his possession is adversed to other co-sharer by any act and conduct. In the instant suit no such evidence has come forward to establish the exclusive title in the property of the plaintiff ousting other co-sharer of the property. 

 14. He argued that admittedly defendant No. 21 purchased some of the property from co-sharers of the plaintiff by different deeds and after purchase he got his name mutated in the khatian. When the defendant No. 21 purchased some of the property from co-sharer of the plaintiff, title of the plaintiff has become clouded, as such, to determine the validity of the deed of the defendant No. 21 and claim of entire suit property by the plaintiff all the co-sharers and all the properties left by Angari Mondal are required to be included into hotchpot. Only taking a portion of the property left by Angari Mondal, it cannot be determined whether there was any amicable arrangement among the co-sharer and what was the quantum of land left by Angari Mondal obtained by other co-sharers. One of the co-sharer cannot claim title over the suit land without bringing all the properties left by Angari Mondal into hotchpot. Therefore, the appellate court rightly held that to get the dispute properly adjudicated upon instant case for simple declaration is not at all maintainable without a prayer for partition of the property and for that reason to enable the plaintiff to get his relief properly adjudicated, giving an opportunity to get his plaint properly amended and to adduce sufficient evidences before the trial court thought it wise and necessary for the interest of justice to sent the case back to the trial court on remand for fresh trial. 

 15. He submits that under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellate court has power to remand the case to the trial court if it finds that the important issue has not been decided properly or the material fact on the part of both the parties have not been incorporated in the pleading. In the instant case, the appellate court rightly found that unless the plaintiff brought a suit for partition along with declaration of title, mere declaration of title in the property will not properly determine the dispute between the parties, as such, the appellate court has not committed any error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 16. He finally argued that the trial court without any relief sought for by the plaintiff, unfortunately observed that all the sale deeds of the defendant No. 21 are void and inoperative and by the said deed, the defendant No. 21 acquired no title in the property, but failed to find that how the plaintiff acquired exclusive title in the property without partition of the suit property. 

 24. I find that the observation regarding execution of the bainanama to some extent true, but this bainanama is not subject matter of the suit. As such, all the observations made by the trial court in respect of execution of bainanama, registration of the same, filing of a suit for Specific performance of Contract are redundant for determination of the dispute between the parties, moreover, bainanama in question was not required to be registered on the date of its execution. In the instant case only question to be decided by the court whether a co-sharer by filing a suit for simple declaration of title on the basis of amicable arrangement among the co-sharer without any written instrument and bringing all other property left by their predecessor into hotchpot can claim title exclusively without filing a suit for partition. 

 25. The trial court did not touch the said question and only relying on the evidence of PWs and one of the DWs came into a finding that the defendant acquired no title in the property by purchase from other co-sharer-defendants, as the bainanama has been created later on to show a contract for sale much earlier than the filing of the suit and said bainanama was required to be registered under the Registration Act, and khatian number mentioned in the sale deed is wrong not attracting the suit property under Khatian No. 18/1. 

 27. The trial court ought to have found that a co-sharer by filing a simple suit for declaration of title for particular quantum of land without partition of the same is not at all entitled to get proper relief. The appellate court while allowing the appeal in its judgment held that; 

 28. Above observations made by the appellate court found to be in consonance with the provision of law and by sending the suit to the trial court on remand for fresh trial, committed no error of law rather the court afforded opportunity to the plaintiff to get the suit properly adjudicated upon suitably amending his plaint and bringing all the property left by Angari Mondal into hotchpot. In the event of proving that other co-sharers got their respective share from other non-suited property left by Angari Mondal in exchange of suit property with the plaintiff by amicable arrangement the plaintiff will succeed and for the reason of remand of the suit, the plaintiff has not in any way deprived from his right, but he will get sufficient opportunity to get his pleading suitably amended and adduce evidences in support of his claim. This question would not have come for adjudication of the present suit if all the co-sharer defendants admitted the claim of the plaintiff like defendant Nos. 3 and 4, but other defendants claiming their title as co-sharers in the property during pendency of the suit transferred some property to the defendant No. 21 which indicates that all the co-sharers did not surrender their share in favour of plaintiff or his father Monser Ali. 

 29. Since some of the co-sharers claiming title in the property transferred the same to the defendant No. 21, title of the co-sharer in the property and validity and legality of their transfer in favour of defendant No. 21 is required to be adjudicated upon in the present suit. For that reason unless all the property left by Angari Mondal is brought into hotchpot simply two plots in its entirety cannot be given to a person who is a co-sharer, in the absence of any partition deed. In a similar situation, the apex court in the case of Tayeb Ali vs Abdul Khalek and others in Civil Appeal No. 42 of 1985 held that, 

 "the suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified share of an undivided plot of land and there being no evidence of exclusive possession at any time, the present suit is not maintainable without a prayer for partition".

parties:
Laila Begum ------ Petitioner
VS
Momtaz Sultana and others --------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
The present opposite party, Momtaz Sultana originally filed the suit seeking following reliefs:— 

 8. Mr. MA Azim Khair, the learned senior counsel along with Mr. Md. Masud Alam, the learned counsel appearing for the defendant No. 3 (ka)- petitioner at the very outset submits that, there has been no scope on the part of the substitute defendants to deviate from their earlier assertion so made in the original written statement filed by their predecessor and therefore the learned judge has misconceively allowed the written statement as well as amendment thereto and therefore the impugned order cannot be sustained. 

 9. The learned counsel by referring to the original written statement so filed by the predecessor of the present petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 2-3 including other defendants who are made as defendant No. 1-4 also contends that, in paragraph 19 to the written statement filed on 23-4-2016 it has categorically been denied the right title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit and prayed for dismissal of the same so in the event of denying title of the plaintiff in the suit the successor of the defendant No. 3 herein the opposite party Nos. 2-3 cannot pray for saham which is tantamount to admitting plaintiff's title over the suit properties. Because if the plaintiff fails to prove her case, the substituted defendant Nos. 2(kha)-2(ga) will not get any saham in the suit land and therefore the written statement and amendment thereto filed by the defendant No. 3(kha) and 3(ga) and allowing so by the impugned order cannot be sustained. 

 13. We have considered the submission so advanced by the learned senior counsel for the petitioner and that of the opposite party No. 1. The point in issue to dispose of the instant Rule is whether by virtue to the written statement filed dated 11-7-2016 and amendment thereto dated 19-11-2018 the opposite party Nos. 3-4 has deviated from their stand made in original written statement filed by their predecessor on 23-4-2016. To adjudicate that very point we have very meticulously gone through the plaint, written statement so filed by the defendant Nos. 1-4, subsequent written statement so filed by the defendant No. 3(kha) and 3(ga) dated 11-7-2016 and that of the amendment to the said written statement dated 19-11-2018. On going through the written statement so filed by the defendant Nos. 3(kha)-3(ga), opposite party Nos. 2-3 we find that, in the prayer portion of the written statement opposite parties prayed for saham to be given along with their mother that is, the petitioner (বিবাদীগণের মাতার অংশের সামিলে বন্টনের বিহিত আজ্ঞা হয়।) but facts remains the mother by adopting the earlier written statement filed by her predecessor and others dated 23-4-2006 prayed for dismissal of the suit. So the prayer so made in the written statement filed dated 11-7-2016 clearly goes opposite to the prayer originally made in the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-4. Furthermore, since the defendants in the original written statement has very robustly challenged the propriety of the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit so under no circumstances can the defendant Nos. 3(kha)- 3(ga) pray for saham which is tantamount to admit the claim of the plaintiff in the suit and therefore the written statement filed subsequently dated 11-7-2016 and that of its amendment dated 19-11-2018 cannot be sustained because if the written statement is allowed the nature and character of the case of the defendants asserted in the original written statement by the defendant Nos. 1-4 will surely be changed.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah

parties:
Md. Abdus Salam ------ Appellant
Vs.
Md Nazrul Islam and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this Civil Appeal are that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Civil Suit No.238 of 2011 impleading the respondents as defendants for a declaration of title in the suit land and also for declaration of Power of Attorney executed by the defendant No.1 being null and void not binding upon the plaintiff also for cancellation of Settlement Case No.01/2005-06. The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, is that the plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun was the original owner of the suit land measuring 01 acre and she got the suit land in. the year 1971-72 pursuant to Settlement Case No. 23(D) of 1971-72 and took over possession of the suit land and paid rent there-of. The government declared the suit land along with its adjacent land as Khas land for establishment of Parjatan Corporation in the year 1982. After establishment of Parjatan Corporation 8.53 acres of land was found in excess which was vested in the Bazar Fund Administration and the same was kept out of the Parjatan Corporation area. Thereafter, a decision was taken for resettlement of the said excess land amongst the affected persons and accordingly 30 decimal of land instead of 1.00 acre was given settlement in the name of the plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun. The plaintiff and his mother went to the concerned office and filed their objection, but did not get any relief. Meanwhile all settlement process in respect of the land of Hill. Districts stopped in the year 1986. The plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun died on 01.06.1984 leaving the plaintiff and one daughter defendant No.2. After the death of the plaintiffs mother, the plaintiff and the defendant No2 had been residing in the suit land with their family members. The defendant No.1 is the son of the defendant No.2 and he created a false Power of Attorney in respect of the suit land to grab the same. The defendant No.1 filed Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 before the Deputy Commissioner and thereafter filed Civil Suit No.72 of 2004 claiming that Mostafa Khatun is the grandmother of the defendant No.1 and the suit land is to be recorded in his name in the Bazar Fund Administration. On 10.01.2005 the Deputy Commissioner directed the concerned official to make settlement in favour of the defendant No.1 in respect of 1.00 acre of land on the priority basis if the settlement process starts again. Thereafter, the defendant No.1 filed Review Miscellaneous Case No.05 of 2008 before the Deputy Commissioner and subsequently upon transfer to the learned Joint District Judge the same was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 which was allowed on 25.05.2009 with a direction to record the suit land in the name of the defendant No.1 under the Bazar Fund Tauzi and accordingly the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendant No.1 through Settlement Case No.01/ 2005-06. Mostafa Khatun died on 01.06.1984 and the defendant No.1 created the Power of Attorney beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff by practicing fraud upon the authority and also got recorded his name in respect of the snit land under the Bazar Fund Tauzi which is illegal and void. The defendant No.1 has concocted the said Power of Attorney to deprive the plaintiff and other heirs of Mostafa Khatun. Thus the title of the plaintiff had become clouded and hence the suit. 

 3. The defendant No.1respondent No.1 contested the suit filing written statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and is barred by limitation. The plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession on the suit land and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit. The suit land was settled in the name of Mostafa Khatun by Settlement Case No.23 (D) of 1971-72 and the same was declared as Khas land on 08.09.1976 by the Deputy Commissioner and vested to the Bazar Fund Administration. The plaintiffs mother executed and registered a bond being No.146/84-85 on 24.07.1984 in favour of the defendant No.l. The defendant No.1 is entitled to get all legal facilities over the movable or immovable properties of Mostafa Khatun by the registered Power of Attorney and accordingly the plaintiff on 05.08.1984 executed a Nadabi Patra in favour of the defendant No.1, thus the defendant No.1 is entitled to get 1.00 acre of land from the Bazar Fund Administration. Subsequently the defendant No.1 filed Civil Suit No.72 of 2004 and obtained an order to be recorded 1.00 acre of land thereby resumed the settlement process. Later on, he filed Review Misc. Case No.05 of 2008 which was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.236 of 2008 and obtained an order directing the Bazar Fund Administration to record his name. The defendant No.1 got the suit land by way of settlement from the Bazar Fund Administration and got his name recorded in the Bazar Fund Tauzi filing Settlement Case No.1/20052006 on 23.06.2009 and since then the defendant No.1 has been possessing the suit land paying rent thereof. The plaintiff did not raise any claim or objection in respect of the suit land even before the Bazar Fund Administration or the concerned Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati Hill District. The land of the plaintiffs predecessor was vested to the Government on 08.09.1976 and as such the plaintiff or his predecessor has no right, title or interest in the suit land. The suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 (4) The Joint District Judge as a court of original jurisdiction, shall try all civil cases in accordance with the existing laws, customs and usages of the districts concerned, except the cases arising out of the family laws and other customary laws of the tribes of the districts of Rangamati, Khagrachori and Bandarban respectively which shall be triable by the Mauza Headmen and Circle Chiefs. 

 26.......  The three districts have been constituted three separate civil jurisdictions under three District Judges and a Joint District judge has been given power to exercise a court of original jurisdiction under section 8(4). While exercising such power he shall follow the existing laws, customs and usages of the districts concerned, except the cases arising out of Family Laws and other customary laws of the tribes of the districts of Rangamati, Khagrachori and Bandarban respectively, which shall be triable by the Mauza headmen and Circle Chiefs. Against an order, judgment or decree passed by the Joint District, the District Judge have been given the appellate power." 

 11. What becomes conspicuous from the above is that by amendment of Section 8 of the Regulation, 1900 by the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Amendment) Act, 2003 Sub-sections (3) (4) and (5) have been added after Sub-section (2). Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 8 provides that Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban shall constitute three separate civil jurisdictions under three District Judges. The Joint District Judge in each hill district as a court of original jurisdiction shall try all civil cases in accordance with the existing laws, customs and usages of the respective district while the cases arising out of the family laws and other customary laws of the tribes in those districts shall be triable by the Mauza Headmen and Circle Chie. According to Sub-section (5) an appeal against the order, judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge shall lie to the District Judge. 

 16. It transpires from the record that the High Court division while making the Rule absolute remanded the original suit to the concerned trial Court for holding trial de novo giving opportunity to the plaintiff and defendant No.1 to prove their respective case by adducing sufficient oral and documentary evidence. The High Court Division observed that the proposition of law is well settled that the averment of plaint and written statement are not admissible as evidence unless corroborated by other oral as well as documentary evidence. It has been further observed that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his case without examining any single witness in support of his case and the trial Court decreed the suit on the basis of documents which were not legally admitted into the evidence. 

 19. Now let us examine how the trial Court decreed the suit. From the record, it appears that admittedly the original owner of the suit land was Mostafa Khatun. The plaintiff appears to claim that by creating a forged Power of Attorney the defendant No.1 obtained an order for correction of the record in Suit No.236 of 2008 and thereafter without getting any relief in Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 the defendant No.1 again with the surreptitious means of using the said Power of Attorney got order of correction of record in his favour in Suit No.72 of 2004 and finally got settlement of the suit land by Settlement Case No.01/05-06. Therefore, the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title in the suit land. 

 20. On examination of the record, it is apparent that the original copy of the said Power of Attorney had not been filed by the defendant No.1. Only a photocopy of the said Power of Attorney was filed from which it appears that the names of the witnesses are illegible. Moreover,' the said Power of Attorney being an unregistered instrument is not admissible in the eye of law as per Section 12 of the Regulation. 

 21. Again, it is evident from the death certificate of Mostafa Khatun that she died on 01.06.1984 at the age of 80 years while the alleged Power of Attorney was created by the defendant No.1 on 24.07.1984 wherein said Mostafa Khatun had been shown as the executant of the same. But practically it is impossible for Mostafa Khatun to execute the alleged Power of Attorney after her death. Therefore, it is crystal clear that the alleged Power of Attorney which is the basis of title of the defendant No.1 is forged and fabricated one and as such the same does not have any evidentiary value in the eye of law. On the other hand, the plaintiff being the son of the original owner of the suit land acquires title in the suit land by way of succession. 

 22. It transpires from the record that the defendant No.1 filed a Nadabipatra dated 05.08.1984 in support of his title. But on going through the said Nadabipatra it divulges that there is no witness in the said document and the discrepancy is patent between the signature of the plaintiff available in the Nadabipatra with the one contained in the plaint. Therefore, it is evident that the said Nadabipatra is forged and fabricated one. In the premises made above, we find that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case and the trial Court on proper appreciation of facts and law decreed the suit while the appellate Court below rightly dismissed the Appeal.

full_judgment:
2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiffs [hereinafter referred to as the appellants] instituted Title Suit No.43 of 1993 in the Court Assistant Judge, Amtoli, Borguna for declaration of the title and recovery of khas possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Abdus Sattar and others. The suit land was sold in auction and the same was purchased by plaintiff No.3 on 30.06.1986 who sold out 6 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 on 14.02.1987 by registered deed. Plaintiff Nos.1 and 3 have been possessing the same by mutating their names in the khatian and paying rent to the Government. Plaintiff No.2 took settlement of 10 decimals of land from plot Nos.921 and 934 recorded in khas khatian No.1 registered by kabuliat dated 12.11.1986 from the Government. In this way, the plaintiffs became the owners of 22 decimals of land. On the 11th day of Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. The plaintiffs requested defendant No.1 to vacate the land, but he did not pay any heed. Hence, the plaintiffs instituted the suit. 

 3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to PS Khatian No.4 of Mouza-Amtoli originally belonged to one Zaminder Zadunath Saha Chowdhury and others who settled 1.81 acres of land to their tenants and kept 1.47 acres of land in their khas possession. One Sukh Lai Saha and others were the owners of the land of PS Khatin No.7 and they settled 2.93 acres of land to the tenants and kept 2.59 acres of land in their khas possession. Zadunath Saha and others through their Naeb Shailendra Nath Sahaettled the land to one Tazem Ali Howlader, the predecessor of defendant No.l. Shailendra Nath executed a salami receipt on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS on behalf of the Zamindars receiving taka 100 as salami from Tazem Ali Howladar. Tazem All Howlader erected dwelling homestead and planted trees etc in the said land. In this way, his father had been a tenant under the Zamindar with regard to 66 decimals of land including the disputed land and thereafter, on 15.01.1960 his father orally gifted him the disputed land by delivering possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing the disputed land since 1960. During revisional survey 1.87 acres of land of PS khatian Nos.4, 7, and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father Tazem Ali Howladar was wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No.1 in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. 

 6. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant-respondents preferred Title Appeal No.19 of 2004 before the District Judge, Barguna. The appeal was transferred to the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Barguna who heard appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Court. 

 9. Ms. Sayeda Nasrin, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, submits that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Government under khas khatian No.1 during SA operation and it vested in the Government and thereafter, the Government settled the suit land in favour of plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 by registered kabuliat vide Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and Lease Case No.02 of AM-1985-86 and thereafter, they mutated their names and paid rent to the Government for the suit land. She further submits that the appellant got settlement of the suit land from the Government by registered kabuliat and got physical possession from the Government and this fact was proved by the plaintiffs by producing both documentary and oral evidence. She further submits that both the Courts below con-currently found the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land pursuant to the settlement case and certificate case and delivery of possession was given by the Government and the concurrent findings of fact as arrived at by both the Courts below are based on material evidence on record. It is finally submitted that there was no misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence on record and the concurrent findings of fact of both the Courts below cannot be interfered by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. 

 10. Per contra, Mr. Shahidul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.1, contends that the plaintiff-appellant totally failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land within 12 years of institution of the suit. He further contends that the fact of settlement allegedly granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barguna in favour of the plaintiffs father vide exhibit-2[Certified copy of Kabuliat dated 12.11.1986] having not proved and allegedly having granted settlement for an unspecified area of .07 decimals out of 1.87 acres of land of Plot No.934, the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was not tenable in Law. He adds that exhibit-3[Certified copy of Boinama of Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and dakhalnama] cannot be construed to be a document of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiff upon an unspecified 07 decimals of land out of 1.87 acres of land when the defendants' two storied dwelling house has been constructed upon a part of Plot No.934. He further contends that Pw-1, in his cross-examination, deposed that 'আমাদের settlement দেয়ার অর্থ দখল দেয়া। যে তারেখেই settlement দেয়া সেই তারিখেই Surveyor আমাদের মেপে জমি বুঝিয়ে দিয়ে আসে।' It is an evidence on oath which clearly disclosed that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit for recovery of khas possession followed by dispossession being out of possession and was not maintainable. He further contends that the evidence adduced by Dw-1 proved it beyond doubt that the defendant has been possessing his homestead, constructed upon a part of the suit plot continuously since 1960. He finally contends that there is no evidence in support of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiffs in the suit land within period from 30.06.1986 to 14.02.1987 and the settlement from the Government dated 12.11.1986 having not proved, the evidence on record proved it beyond doubt that the plaintiffs instituted the suit being out of possession. 

 12. The claim of the plaintiff-appellants is that they are the owners of the land by Nilam purchase and by purchasing with consideration money vide registered kabala and kabuliyat from the owners of the land, i.e. from the Government as khas land lease and they possessed the land. Devastating Tornedo and flood washed away their house, so the land remained vacant. When WAPDA cut mud from there, a ditch was made therein where the defendant erected houses illegally, forcibly dispossessing the plaintiffs from 'Ka' scheduled land on 11 Falgoon, 1396 BS. A local salish was held wherein the defendants admitted that they would hand over possession. The land in question has properly been recorded in the name of the plaintiffs when the defendant has failed to mutate his name and his rather also failed to mutate his name in the disputed khatian. The plaintiffs claimed that they have been able to prove their right, title and interest in the suit land by producing parchas, boinama, dakhalnama, kabuliyat, rent receipts which are public documents. In support of their contention, they cited the cases: Brahma Nand Puri-Vs-Neki Puri, reported in AIR1965SC1506 and Vijay Pullarwar-Vs-Shri Hanuman Deostan, (2019)11SCC718. 

 13. On the other hand, the defendant-respondents claim that their predecessor, Tazem Ali Hawlader got pattan of 39 decimals of land of P.S. Plot No.42 under P.S. Khatian No.4 and 27 decimals of land of P.S. Plot No.42 under P.S. Khatian No.7, i.e. total 66 decimals of land from Lakhmikol Barobari Estate through a Naeb on 5 Baishak, 1359 vide printed receipt of the Estate for taka 100'00 as appropriate salami and got dakhila on 15.08.1960 BS by paying taka 26 as rent. Said Tazem Ali Hawlader gifted the said land orally to defendant No.1 and since then he has been possessing the land erecting house and planting trees and digging a pond nursing fish therein. The plaintiffs have got no title and possession in the suit land. In deposition, defendant No.1 also stated that his father on 15'" January, 1960 orally gifted him 66 decimals of land. At that time, all the heirs of his father were present. The cyclone blown on April, 1961 destroyed his homestead and he re-built the same by his own expense. 

 14. Defendant No.1 also claimed that during Revisional Survey operation, 26 decimals of land of P.S.Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 is neither recorded in the name of any landlord nor in any other name at all, but recorded in the names of Amrita Lal, Abdul Aziz and others, Kali Bilash and Keshab Lal and others in S.A. Khatian Nos.22/261/411 and 427 correctly. 1'87 acres of land of PS Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father, Tazem Ali Hawlader wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No. 1 in the name of Government. Having taken the opportunity of the wrong record, the Revenue Officer of Amtali Upazila declared for pattan on 01.11.1393 B.S. and to save the possession of defendant No.1, he filed Title Suit No. 34 of 1987 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and on transfer, it was renumbered as Title Suit No.8 of 1992 which was heard and dis-missed on 15.08.1992 by the learned Assistant Judge, Bamna Upazila, Borguna. Against the judgment and order, defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.56 of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Borguna which is still pending. 

 15. The claim of title and possession to the suit land has two dimensions. The plain-tiffs claim title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land, on the basis of auction purchase, boinama, dhakhalnama, sale deed and lease from the Government in pursuance of settlement case and kabuliayat. Conversely, defendant No.1 claims title and possession to the suit land on the basis of Salami receipt, rent receipts and oral gift from his father Tazem Ali Hawlader. The burden of proof as per Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act, 1872 primarily rests upon the plaintiffs to prove their claims. Rules 1 and 2 of Order-XVIII of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 also provides that the plaintiff has right to begin and shall produce his evidence in support of the issues which he is bound to prove. 

 16. On perusal of the documents on record, it appears that 12 decimals of land of Plot No.935 of SA Khatian No.789 under Amtalimouza belong to Abdus Sattar, Birendra Bijoy Das and others. The aforesaid land was auctioned on 30.06.1986 and plaintiff No. 3 purchased the same. On 14.02.1987, plaintiff No.3 by a registered deed of sale transferred six decimals of land of Plot No.935 to plain-tiff No. l. Plaintiff Nos.3 and 1 mutated their names. Bijendra Bijoy Das, father of plaintiff No.3 achieved pattan of 3 decimals of land of Plot No.921 and 7 decimals of land of Plot No.934 in total 10 decimals of land from khas khatian No.1 of the Government through Settlement Case No.2(Am) of 1985-86. A Kabuliyat deed was registered on 12.11.1986 after having salami of taka 1750 and a new khatian No. 1326 was created in the name of Birendra Bijoy Das. The plaintiffs exhibited original parcha of SA khatian No.1326, certified copy of Kabuliyat dated 12.1.1.1986, the boinama and dakhalnama of certificate case No. 827(Am) of 1980-81, DCR of payment of salami taka 1.750 dated 10.11.1986, certified copy of SA Khatian No.789 and certified copies of order sheet of Settlement Case No.2(Am)/ 85-86.In the instant suit, the plaintiffs have produced documentary evidence, most of which are public in nature, regarding their title to the suit land. They also produced documentary evidence dhakhalnama and rent receipts in support of their possession to the suit land before dispossession. Simultaneously, they produced oral evidence in support of their title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that Pw-1 consistently deposed in support of the plaint that they took possession of the suit land in accordance with certificate case, boinama, dakhalnama, sale deed, and kabuliyat but on 23'02/1990 corresponding to 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.E. Defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit lard by force. Pw-1 did not depose contrary to his statement during cross-examination. Pw-2 and Pw-3 duly corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 regarding the plaintiffs' title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land. It appears that Pw-2 materially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 to the effect that on 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Likewise, Pw-3 substantially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 that during 1396 B.S. defendant no 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. It appears that the plaintiffs have primarily been able to prove their title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land and they have discharged their initial burden of proof. Now it is the turn of defendant No.1 to discharge his onus of proof. In terms of Section 102 of the Evidence act, 1872, the initial onus to prove its claim is always on the plaintiff and if he discharges that onus and makes out a case which entitles him to a relief, the onus shifts to the defendant to prove these circumstances, if any, which would disentitle the plaintiff to the same [Bharat Alumnium Co.-V- Maharashtra Alumnium Co., 2009 DLT 489]. In a suit for possession based on title once the plaintiff has been able to create a high degree of probability so as to shift the onus on the defendant, it is for the defendant to discharge his onus and in the absence thereof, the burden of proof lying on the plaintiff shall be held to have been discharged so as to amount to proof of the plaintiffs title [R. V. E. Venkatachala Gounder -V- Arulmigu Viswesaraswaini and V. P. Temple, AIR 2003 SC 4548]. Let us have an overview of the defendant's case to see defendant No.1 has been able to discharge his onus of proof. 

 17. The disputed land is presently situated at Amtali Upazila of Borguna District which was formerly included in the subdivision of Patuakhali. Defendant No.1 in support of his title to the suit land produced an unregistered salami receipt dated 5 Baishakh, 1359. BS and Dakhila dated 15.08.1360 BS. The trial Court and the Appellate Court were of the view that at date of execution of the salami receipts on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS corresponding to 18th April 1952 AD Zamindari system was not prevalent because of the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) and, therefore, Zamindars had no right to give pattan of their land at that time. But the High Court Division took a different view on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act stating that Part-V of this Act came into force in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 AD. The view taken by the High Court Division on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act appears to be correct since Part-V of the SAT Act came into force in entire area of Patuakhali Sub-Division of the District of Bakcrganj with effect from the date of publication of the notification in the Dacca Gazette, vide Notification No.9918-LR., date 8th July 1954, published in the Decca Gazette, date 5th August, 1954, Part-I, p. 890 (SAT ACT DLR by Obaidul Huq Chowdhury, Fifth Edition-2015, page 242- 243].Hence, in the Subdivision of Patuakhali Zamindars had right to give pattan of their land by receiving salami before 5th August, 1954. But the question pertaining to this case is whether Naeb Shailendra Nath Saha executing the salami receipt on behalf of the Zamindars gave the same to the father of defendant No.1, Tazem Ali Hawlader and delivered possession of the suit land to him or not? The salami receipts and rent receipts were marked as exhibits with objection. Salami receipt and dakhila are private documents and those will not be admissible in evidence as genuine documents on the mere production of the same. The genuineness of the salami receipt has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The Appellate Court held that the salami receipt/lease document is not genuine itself since it is rubbed and has cut marks and the back page of it is covered by white paper. This view of the Appellate Court regarding the title document of defendant No.1 seems to be based on proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the case of Ajufannessa @ AjiBibi and others-Vs-Safar Miah and others, 30 D.L.R (AD) 41 it was held that "A private document can-not be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case." The ratio of this case was again reiterated in the case of Md. Jashimuddins Kanchan -Vs- Md. Ali Ashraf (42 DLR (AD) 289]. The High Court Division did not reverse this finding of the Appellate Court that the genuineness of the salami receipt is highly doubtful. Since the tide document of the father of defendant No.1 is highly doubtful, subsequent transfer of the same property to defendant No.1 by oral gift is also doubtful. Defendant No.1 claimed that during 1961 his house at the disputed land was destroyed by cyclone for which he repaired the same with his own expense. But he deposed,  “১৯৬১ সালে আমি ৬ষ্ঠ শ্রেণীতে পড়তাম। তখন আমার ব্যক্তিগত আয়ের উৎস ছিলনা।" This portion of the deposition of Dv-1 suggests that the claim of defendant No.1 regarding his possession of the suit property from 1960 onward is apparently baseless. It appears that father of defendant No.1 and thereafter, defendant No.1 did not take any time worthy step whatsoever for correction of the record of rights. The possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land cannot be traced back to any valid title whereas the possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs in the suit land can be traced back to valid title which coupled with attending facts and circumstances reasonably gives rise to the presumption that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land by defendant No.1 by force. 

 19. Upon perusal of the Judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division on erroneous belief decided the case keeping in view of section-9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. But the pleadings of the parties clearly indicate that this case is brought under section-8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 read with Article 142 of schedule-1 to the Limitation Act, 1908 and, therefore, the plaintiffs case file the suit for recovery of possession within 12 years from the date of dispossession. The finding by the High Court Division to the effect that the notice by the government to defendant No.1 to vacate possession cast a substantial doubt in believing the plaintiffs' case does not seem to be correct since possession of defendant No.1 can never be adverse to the government without defendant No. 1 is 60 years continuous adverse possession as per article 149 of schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which is absent in the present case. 18. The trial Court as well as the Appellate Court arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title and possession following by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that the findings of the trial court as well as the Appellate Court are based on the proper appreciation of evidence on record both oral and documentary. It is well settled position in law that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court cannot re-appreciate the evidence and cannot set aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below by taking a different view of the evidence. The High Court is empowered only to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are per-verse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below. Simply because another view of the evidence may be taken is no ground by the High Court to interfere in its revisional jurisdiction [Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. The civil cases are decided on the basis of preponderance of probability. Civil cases are decided on the basis of pre-ponderance of evidence while in a criminal case the entire burden lies on the prosecution and proof beyond reasonable doubt has to be given [Vishnu Dutt Sharma-V-Daya Sapra 13 SCC (2009) page 729]. In view of the facts, circumstances and proposition of law discussed above, we are of the view that the preponderance of probability regarding title and possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs to the suit land is clearly in favour of the plaintiffs and, therefore, the High Court Division made serious error of law in making the rule absolute which occasioned failure of justice.

parties:
Mosammat Ayesha Akhter Begum ------ Appellant
Vs.
Nuruzzaman and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Civil Appeal are that the appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.123 of 1991 against the respondents for declaration of title in the suit land. The case of the plaintiff, in a nutshell, is that one Ram Chandra Dey got settlement of the suit land vide N.H.C.C. Settlement Case No.216 of 1941-42 and executed Kabuliyat in favour of the government and accordingly the same was accepted and Khatian No.860 was opened in the name of said Ram Chandra Dey. While possessing and enjoying the suit land said Ram Chandra Dey died leaving behind Chinta Haran Dey as only son. Chinta Haran Dey sold out the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 and handed over possession of the same to the plaintiff. The plaintiff had been possessing and enjoying the suit land by cultivation with the knowledge of the defendants and other people. The defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit land since then. The plain-tiff was informed that the suit land was recorded in the name of vendor of the plaintiff and the deed would be written accordingly. Thereafter the plaintiff came to know that during Diara Survey the suit land was not recorded in the name of vendor of the plaintiff rather the same wrongly recorded in the name of the predecessor of the defendants No.1-11, Abid Ali and others and in the name of the defendants No.12 and 13, which cast doubt cloud on the title of the plaintiff. The plaintiff on 12.02.1989 sent one Siraj (her nephew) to the concerned Tahsil Office to pay rent of the suit lana and came to know from said Siraj about the wrong record of the suit land in the name of defendant, thereafter, the plain-tiff collected the certified copy of the Khatian and learnt properly about the wrong record of the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title. 

 3. The defendant No.12-respondent No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the defendant No.12 is the owner of the suit land measuring 4.20 acres along with other non-suit land. One Ram Chandra Dey got settlement of the said land vide N.H.S.C. No.216 of 1941-42 and accordingly the Kabuliyat was executed in the name of Ram Chandra Dey and Khatian No.860 was recorded in his name. Ram Chandra Dey gave settlement of the suit land to the father of the defendant No.12 at his proposal and subsequently Ram Chandra Dey executed Patta dated 12th Baishakh, 1385 B.S. and handed over possession of the suit land to the father of the defendant No.12. The father of the defendant No.12 used to possess the suit land on his behalf and thereafter the defendant No.12 used to possess the same through Bargadar. The defendant No.12 is sole owner of the suit land under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. During the Diara survey the defendant No.12 was in belief that Diara khatian regarding the suit land was correctly recorded in his name, but after receiving the summons of the suit and copy of Diara Khatian No.333 the defendant came to know that only 5(five) annas share out of 16(sixteen) annas of the suit land recorded in the name of defendant No.12. The husband of the plaintiff namely Abdul Khaleque was the clerk and posted at Diara operation office at Ramgati and the defendant No.13, Abdur Rahim was the peon of the said office and they in connivance with each other taking the privilege of being the employee of Diara Office got illegally recorded the rest portion of the suit land in the name of the defendant No.13 Abdur Rahim and father, brother and other sister of said Abdul Khaleque although they have no right, title or possession of the suit land. Ram Chandra Dey had no son namely Chinta Haran Dey, but the plaintiff created the forged deed by showing a fictitious person. The valuation of the land was Tk.1,00,000.00 at the time of alleged transfer of the suit land, but the plaintiff created a forged deed stating the valuation of the suit land at Tk.5,000.00 only. The husband of the plaintiff is witness of the so-called deed and Diara plot was not mentioned in the said deed and the possession of the suit land was never handed over to the plaintiff. Ram Chandra Dey left the country and went to India and he never came back to this country and the cause of action of the suit land did not arise on 16.02.1989. The defendant No.12 has been possessing and enjoying the total suit land of plot No.1336 including the non-suit land for more than 12 years and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 13. On scrutiny of the record, it is seen that the plaintiff filed the registered sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 which was marked as Exhibit-2. The said sale deed being a registered deed executed by the successor of the original owner generally does not put any hindrance to pass title to the vendee i.e. plaintiff. Yet the main contention between the plaintiff and the defendant No.12 is whether the vendor namely Chinta Haran Dey is son of Ram Chandra Dey and the aforesaid sale deed was executed fraudulently with false personation. 

 16. From the Exhibit-6 i.e. certified copy of the death register it appears that Ram Chandra Dey died in Bangladesh on 25.09.1960 at Omarpur, Police Station-Sudharam, District-Noakhali and the information of his death was registered on 17.10.1960. P.W.5 stated in his cross-examination that they had two houses and his father-in-law's house at Omarpur was merged in the river erosion, thereafter his father built house at Sonapur. P.W.5 was cross-examined by the defendant No.12, but no discrepancy was made. Apart from this, P.W.3 deposed that at the time of execution of sale deed (Exhibit-2) he was present. This witness identified his signature in the said deed as Exhibit-2(Ka). P.W.3 was cross-examined by the defendant No.12 but no contradiction could have been shown. Thus, P.Ws.1, 3 and 5 deposed coherently supporting the title of the plaintiff in the suit land. 

 17. In view of the discussion made above, it is abundantly clear that Ram Chandra Dey never left the country for India and he died in the country leaving Chinta Haran Dey as the only son due to which the sale deed No.20095 dated 27.12.1984 (Exhibit-2) executed by Chinta Haran Dey is genuine and the plaintiff accrued legal title in the suit land by virtue of the said sale deed. 

 18. On the other hand, the defendant No.12 claims his title on the footing that Ram Chandra Dey gave settlement of the suit land in his favour at Tk.80.00 as Salami and accordingly Diara Khatian No.333 was finally prepared in his name. The defendant No.12 filed unregistered Patta deed (Exhibit-Ka) in support of his claim. But regarding the authenticity of Exhibit-Ka the appellate Court observed in the following: 

 22. In the given backdrop, it is abundantly proved that Patta (Exhibit-Ka) adduced by the defendant No.12 is a false and fabricated document which did not confer a valid title on the defendant No.12, hence we are of the view that the defendant No.12 has not acquired any valid title on the basis of the said Patta. 

 27. In view of the discussion made above, the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land is proved without controversy and the trial Court on proper appreciation of the relevant facts decreed the suit and the lower appellate Court also finding no anomaly upheld the judgment of the trial Court.
