full_judgment:
The sole plaintiff, Mosammat Hilufa Hanum Joarder filed Title Suit No. 302 of 1976 for declaration of her title, recovery of possession and also for mesne profits in respect of 0.29 acre of suit property including the building and structures standing thereon know as 'Acharya Lodge' along with mesne profit of Taka 7,06,000. The above title suit was lastly renumbered as Title Suit No. 73 of 1984. 

 4. The sole plaintiff also filed Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 for declaration that, order of requisition dated 26-5-1964 passed by the Extra-Assistant Commissioner and Land Acquisition collector, Kushtia in LA Case No. 12/63-64 in respect of 0.29 acre of suit property with building and structures thereon at Chuadanga town, and dispossession of the plaintiff therefrom were illegal and also for directing the defendants to restore her the suit property and possession along with payment of adequate co-operation for damages. The above title suit was lastly re-numbered as Title Suit No. 117 of 1981, and thereafter, Title Suit No. 24 of 1988 respectively. 

 5. The plaintiff also filed Title Suit No. 88 of 1972 for declaration that, the order of permanent acquisition dated 8-6-1966 relating to the plaintiff's 'Acharya Lodge' is illegal, Mak fide, collusive, fraudulent, inoperative, and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for direction to restore the vacant possession of the same. The above title suit was lastly re-numbered as Title Suit No. 141 of 1984. 

 6. The plaintiff is the owner in possession of the building and other structures standing on 0.29 acre of the land in CS Plot Nos. 2203 and 2210 under Khatian Nos. 218 and 298 of Mouza Chuadanga in Chuadanga town in the District of Kushtia. The plaintiff acquired the property and obtained possession over it firstly on the basis of a Bainapatra dated 18-12-1963 and subsequently, by Kabala dated 16-1-1964 from the owner Md Mahbub Hossain, the lawful owner in possession, who had acquired the same by exchange from the heirs of CS recorded tenant Upendra Nath Acharjee. In such position, defendant No. 2, the Extra-Assistant Commissioner issued an order of requisition of the suit property dated 25-5-1964 for providing accommodation to the branch office of the National Bank of Pakistan in the Town of Chuadanga District, addressing the plaintiff's husband, who was an officer of the then Government of East Pakistan, and had been working as a Circle Officer in different outlying areas of the country. In 1964, the plaintiff's husband was serving at Kishoregonj Sub-Division. Though the Bank had its existing office in a proper place in the town, yet requisition and acquisition was done with ulterior motive without serving any notice to the plaintiff. No sooner had the plaintiff come to know the matter, than he raised objection to defendant No. 2, and preferred an appeal to the Commissioner, lamina Division, and thereafter, to the Government through the Secretary, Revenue Department on 26-12-1964, but, they did not give any reply. After that, the plaintiff filed an application on 1-1-1966 to the Minister-in-Charge of Revenue where the plaintiff's application for vacating the order of requisition was rejected, and she was intimated through a letter dated 23-9-1965. Lastly, the plaintiff's prayer for review was also rejected by a letter dated 12-11-1965. After that, the plaintiff had submitted her original unregistered 'Bainapatra' in support of her transaction following the subsequent possession from its lawful owner and title holder of the suit property by exchange within the knowledge of defendant Nos. 1-3. But no notice was ever served on either of them under the provisions of East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of property Act, while the plaintiff was thrown out of her own property most arbitrarily. The Order of permanent acquisition dated 8-6-1966 was disclosed for the first time on 7-11-1970, and the defendant in their written statement in Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 admitted the same, and following the requisition order, defendant No. I forcibly took possession of the suit property on 21-11-1965 after evicting the plaintiff, and in that aspect, the cause of action in Title Suit No. finally arose on 12-11-1965, when the defendants refused to interfere with requisition order made by defendant No.3's Head Office at Dhaka, and also filed Title Suit No. 

 7. Defendant Nos.1-3, contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaints. Their cases, in short, are that, the plaintiff was not the owner of the suit property, requisitioned under HR Case No. 12/63-64, and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13/65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of the National Bank of Pakistan, Chuadanga Branch, where the plaintiff failed to produce any documents of her ownership. The acquisition notices under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant. The acquisition notices under section 5(1A) and 5(3) were issued, and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively, where advance payment was offered on 31-5-1966, but the owners did not appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian nationals. The plaintiff has no locus standi or right, title and possession over the suit property. The permanent acquisition of the suit property is neither illegal nor void. The suit is not maintainable as the LA proceeding has been finalized long before, and no suit against an order passed or any action taken under Emergency Requisition Property Act was maintainable. 

 8. Defendant No.4, National Bank Limited, also contested the suit by filling written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. Its case, in short, is that there is no cause of action against the defendant, and the suit is barred by limitation. The defendant does not admit the title of the plaintiff, and also of her predecessor Mahbub Hossain. The property was requisitioned on 26-5-1964 for public interest, and public purpose. The plaintiff failed to prove her title over the suit property, where the requisition notice was also issued on SA recorded tenants, and the said notice was also served upon the husband of the plaintiff as he had possessing the house at the time of requisition. The defendant No.4 got possession on 21-11-1965. The suit is not maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition Act, 1948, and, as such, the defendant prayed for dismissing the suit. 

 13. Mr Sk Md Morshed, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants in all the appeals, submits that, the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No. 12/63-64 and permanently acquired through LA Case No.13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, the High Court Division erred in modifying the decree of the Trail Court regarding title of the property. He further submits that, the requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant and acquisition notices under sections 5(IA) and 5(3) were issued, and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively, and advanced payment was offered on 31-5-1966 and the owners failed to appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian Nationals, and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding reassessment of compensation according to the present market value. He then submits that, the plaintiff having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, and having no locus standi, and the LA proceeding having been finalized long before, and no objection having been taken against the said acquisition under Emergency Requisition of Property Act, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court. He lastly submits that, the suit of the plaintiff not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1984, and the plaintiff having failed to establish her ownership of the suit property, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree passed by the Trail Court, and, as such, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division being not sustainable, and, the same is liable to be set-aside. Hence, he prayed that, the instant appeals may kindly be allowed. 

 14. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in all the cases submits that, the plaintiff acquired valid title by virtue of a deed of agreement, and by subsequent Kabala, and, as such, she became the owner of the property in question, then the finding and observation passed by the High Court Division in decreeing in the Title Suit No. 302 of 1976 may be sustained, and, hence, the High Court rightly passed the impugned judgment. He further submits that, the High Court Division passed an order directing the defendant appellants herein to reconsider the compensation on the assessment of the same for the purpose of permanent acquisition, but, to that, expect to judgment and order dated 4-6-2009 by the High Court Division was correct, and, legal. He finally submits that, the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division was legal as the instant suit was maintainable as per provision of Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and, therefore, he prays for dismissal of the instant appeals. 

 15. Mr MA Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 in Civil Appeal No. 194 of 2014 submits that, the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No.12/63-64, and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for the accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (Now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, Proforma Respondent No. 2 (defendant No. 4), and who got possession on 21-11-1965, and requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant, and the acquisition novice under section 5(IA) and 5(3) of the Act, 1948, and served on 8-6-1966 and 31-5-1966, and owners failed to appear to receive the advance money as they were Indian Nationals. He further submits that, suits of the plaintiff are misconceived not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. He finally submits that, the plaintiff failed to prove her title over the suit property where the requisition notice was also issued on SA recorded tenants, and the said notice was also served upon the husband of the plaintiff as he had been possessing the house at the time of requisition. The impugned judgment passed by the High Court Division is illegal and not maintainable. Hence, the same is liable to be set-aside. 

 "Mr Abdus Salam, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the leave-petitioners in all the petitions for leave to appeal, submits that the plaintiff not being the owner of the property requisitioned under HR Case No..12/63-64 and permanently acquired through LA Case No. 13 of 65-66 which was requisitioned for accommodation of National Bank of Pakistan (now Sonali Bank Limited), Chuadanga Branch, the High Court Division erred in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding title of the property. He further submits that the requisition notice under section 3 was issued on SA recorded tenant and acquisition notices under sections 5(1A) and 5(3) were issued and served on 8-6-1966 and 9-6-1966 respectively and advance payment was offered on 31-5-1966 and the owners failed to appear to receive the advance payment as they were Indian Nationals and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court regarding reassessment of compensation according to the present market value. He then submits that the plaintiff having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property and having no locus standi and the LA proceeding having been finalized long before and no objection having been taken against the said acquisition under Emergency Requisition of Property Act, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree of the Trial Court. He lastly submits that the suit of the plaintiff not being maintainable under section 14A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and the plaintiff having failed to establish her ownership in the suit property, the High Court Division erred in law in modifying the decree passed by the trial Court." 

 "Once the property is acquired and gazette notification is published under section 5(7) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (Act XIII of 1948), the right, title and interest if any of the owners are extinguished and preparation of Khatian or payment of rent does not improve the position of the original owners in respect of acquired land." 

 20. In this case there is dispute of title as well as non-acceptance of compensation as assessed by the Deputy Commissioner concerned. However, there are provisions for settling these sorts of disputes as per section 7 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. As per sub-section (aaa) read with sub-section (b) these disagreements should be resolved by the Arbitrator appointed for these purposes and against the Arbitrator's Award, an appeal could be preferred to the High Court Division. 3. The case of the plaintiffs in short is that Abdul Meah was the original RS recorded owner of the suit land, who died leaving his only son namely, Bazal Ahmed; that the said Bazal Ahmed died leaving behind one wife Mazema Khatun, one son Emdadul Islam and two daughters Nur Nahar Begum and Shamsun Nahar Begum; that the aforesaid heirs of Bazal Ahmed had been in possession in the suit land on due payment of necessary rents and taxes to the Government; that the suit property was put in auction through certificate Case No. 3496/60-61 for arrear rent and on payment of arrear rent by the heirs of Bazal Ahmed, the certificate case came to an end on 16-2-1961; that by a registered kabala dated 28-10-1963 Majena Khatun, Emdadul Islam and Nurun Nahar Begum transferred 24 sataks of land to Reja Mia and Kamal Uddin; that thereafter Majena Khatun, Emdadul Islam and Nurun Nahar Begum by a registered sale deed dated 3-9-1970 transferred 12 sataks of land to Mohammad Mia and thereafter, Raja Meah by registered sale deed dated 24-10-1970 transferred his aforesaid purchased land to Noman; that Kamal Uddin by registered sale deed dated 10-11-1969 transferred 10 sataks of land to Syed Fazal Ahmed and Syed Ahmmed Hoque and thereafter Noman transferred 6 sataks of land to Maklesur Rahman by sale deed dated 22-1-1971; that Noman and Moklesur Rahman by registered sale deed dated 22-7-1978 transferred 12 sataks of land to Nurun Nahar Begum; that thereafter Mohammad Meah Chowdhury by sale deed dated 23-3-1978 transferred 5 gondas, 3 koras of land to plaintiff No. 1; that said Nur Nahar Begum transferred 4 gondas of land to plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 by sale deed dated 8-2-1979; that Nur Nahar Begum transferred 2 gondas of land to plaintiff No. 4 by sale deed dated 9-2-1979 and the aforesaid Fazlul Ahmad and Aminul Hogue by sale deed dated 10-7-1979 transferred 6 gondas of land to plaintiff No. 5. Thereafter, the heirs of Bazal Ahmad namely Shamsun Nahar, Nurun Nahar, Mayena Khatun, Emdadul Islam transferred rest of their 5 gondas of land to plaintiff No.5 and in this way the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land by purchase through several purchase deeds by erecting houses on conversion of the null land into vhiti land on payment of due taxes to the Government. Thereafter, the plaintiffs constructed residential house and tenanted house in the suit land and have been possessing and enjoying the same; that the plaintiffs installed tube well in the suit property and also planted vegetable garden on vacant land; that the defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit land; that during PS operation the PS khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of one Abdul Bashar, who was a Karjakarak of the vendor of plaintiffs and thereafter BS khatian was correctly prepared in the name of the heirs of Bazal Ahmad; that the defendants are powerful men in locality having militant forces; that the defendant Nos. 1-3 by their hired `gundas' tried to illegally evict the plaintiffs and thereupon, the plaintiffs filed Criminal Case; that at the influence of defendants the officer-in-charge of local Police Station arrested the plaintiff No. 5 on 26-8-1980 and created pressure upon the plaintiffs for surrendering possession of the suit land to defendants and thereby the plaintiffs instituted the suit by mentioning cause of action on 6-8-1980 and 26-8-1980; that due to institute of the suit, the powerful defendants during continuation of Martial law regime issued notice to predecessor of plaintiffs SM Kamal Uddin for appearance before the Martial Law Administrator and on appearance before the Martial Law Administrator, who instructed to SM Kamal Uddin to hand over possession of the suit land by making demarcation through a survey knowing Advocate. Since SM Kamal Uddin did not comply with such illegal instruction, he was given a second notice on 10-7-1982 for appearance before Martial Law authority and before the said date of appearance Kamal Uddin died by suffering serious mental agony; that thereafter on 9-6-1982 the prayer for mandatory injunction was incorporated as the defendants constructed house in some portion of the suit land during pendency of the suit by amending the plaint. 

 4. The defendant Nos. 1-5, 7-8 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the defendants have right, title and possession in 34 sataks of land in RS plot No. 1172 under RS khatian 615; that original owner of the suit land was Abdul Meah, who died leaving son Bazal Ahmed; that Majma Khatun; Bazal Ahmed died leaving behind wife Majma Khatun, who married Rashid Ahmed and both of them used to live in the domain of Bazal Ahmed as husband and wife; that Rashid Ahmed, Majma Khatun gave birth one son Emdadul Islam, two daughters named Nurun Nahar and Shamsun Nahar; that the suit property was put to auction for arrear rents through CC No. 1937(A)-1946-47 and auction purchased by Syed Ahmed of Chakaria on 14-10-1947 and got possession through Court on 6-2-1978; Syed Ahmed after getting possession of the suit land died leaving behind 4 sons namely Jashim Uddin, Nasir Uddin, Monir Uddin, Hasan Ahmed and one wife namely, Sajeda Begum; that the heirs of Syed Ahmed instituted Misc. Case No. 106/63-64 before the CO Revenue for demarcation of the property of RS plot No. 1172 corresponding to PS plot No. 438; that during preparation of PS record the name of one Abdul Bashar was wrongly recorded with Syed Ahmed and the heirs of Syed Ahmed by filing Appeal No. 45/62 corrected their names and accordingly their names were inserted; that the plaintiffs and their vendors cannot claim any title in the suit land as their right was extinguished through auction sale in 1946; that the transfer deeds shown by the plaintiffs are false and fraudulent and those were not acted upon; that Jasimuddin and others transferred the property of suit plot No. 1172 to the defendants by executing 7 deeds dated 1-8-1980 and delivered possession; that the defendants duly paid revenue and taxes to the Government; that the suit property was basically a tank and the heirs of Syed Ahmed by earth filling developed the land into vhiti land and the defendants erected two katcha house in the northern side; that on 20-8-1980 while the plaintiffs broken the said 2 katcha house, the defendant filed Panchalis Police Station Case No. 16(8)80 and before institution of the present suit the defendants erected a katcha house in southern side of the suit land; that the plaintiffs amalgamated RS plot No. 1173 with RS plot No. 1172; that the plaintiffs have no right title and possession in the suit land; that the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 4-7 filed an additional written statement stating, inter alia, that the facts alleged in the application for amendment of plaint are not correct; that the defendant did not influence Martial Law authority during continuation of Martial Law regime; that the cause of Martial Law harassment to the predecessor of plaintiffs by defendants by issuance of notices are not correct. The plaintiffs filed the suit on false averments and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 9. Mr Omar Faruk, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners in the course of argument takes me through the plaint, exhibited document, judgments of 2 Courts below and other materials on record and then submits that the plaintiff purchased the suit property by 5 registered deeds being registered deed dated 23-3-1978 , 8-2-1979 , 9-2-1979, 10-12-1979 and 11-12-1979 (Exhibited documents.) and since the date of purchase the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land by paying rent to the Government in accordance with law although during pendency' of the suit the defendants with some miscreants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs on 18-1-1981 from the suit land although the Court of appeal below without considering the fact that during pendency of the suit the defendants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land most illegally set-aside the well founded judgment of the trial Court below, which resulted in the failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiffs to prove his case examined 3 witnesses out of which PW 1, PW 2 and PW 3 in their respective evidence categorically stated that the plaintiffs are the real owner of the suit land and they possessed the suit land. Finally, the learned Advocate submits that the plaintiffs to prove their right, title and possession in the suit land exhibited a series of documents namely, Exhibit 1 (RS khatian No. 615), Exhibit 1 (a) (RS khatian No. 681), Exhibit 2 (dakhila of original owner), Exhibit 2(a), 2(b)-(rent receipt of original owner of khatian No. 615), Exhibit 2(c), 2(d), 2(e)-(rent receipt of original owner of khatian No. 681), Exhibit 3 (Certificate Objection Case No. 3496/ 60-61), Exhibit 4 to 4(k) (deeds) etc. although the Court of appeal below giving a goby to such material evidence on record abruptly arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs could not prove their prima-facie title and possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate to fortify his submission has relied on the decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 75. 

 18. These being purely a finding of fact based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record. Therefore, I find no reason to differ with Cie view taken by the Court of appeal below. The law is by now well settled that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiffs shall have to prove the exclusive possession in the suit land in order to get a decree. The Court may incidentally enquire into the prima-facie title of the parties. in this case, I have already noticed that the plaintiffs having failed to prove their possession in the suit land.

2. The land measuring an area of 0.40 acre appertaining to CS Khatian No.6359 and Plot No.16 originally belonged to Sheikh Kitabdi, who acquired title in the same by executing a kabuliyat on 24-4-1906 in favour of the landlords Girish Chandra Poddar and others. They sold 5 kathas of land to one Jakir Hossain by a deed dated 27-12-1969 who transferred 2½ kathas to Abdul Musabbir Hossain, father of the writ petitioners by another deed dated 20-4-1970. The BTMC preferred Appeal Case No. 27938 of 2000, which was also dismissed. The BTMC, then, filed an application for re-hearing of the appeal before the Settlement Officer which was again dismissed on 20-3-2007 along with 26 appeals. Then, the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.10535 of 2007 and obtained Rule which was made absolute by the impugned judgment and order. 

 3. The CS recorded tenant Sheikh Kitabdi died leaving his two daughters Arjuda Begum and Meher Nigar.  4. One Kalachand Sheikh was the owner and possessor of the land measuring 0.31 acre by virtue of a kabuliyat dated 20-4-1906 which was duly recorded in CS khatian No.6196 and plot No.15. The writ petitioners, then, filed Writ Petition No.2687 of 2010 against the order dated 22-8-2007 passed by the Charge Officer in Appeal Case No.27957 of 2000 and obtained Rule. The said Rule was made absolute by the impugned judgment and order. 

 5. The land measuring an area of 0.31 acre appertaining in CS khatian No.6196 and plot No.15 originally belonged to Kalachand Sheikh who got the same by executing kabuliyat deed dated 24-4-1906. He, died leaving two daughters Ramjan Bewa and Marium Bewa. Thereafter, Mariam died leaving Falu Mia as her only heir. Ramjan Bewa and Falu Mia sold 0.10 acre of land from the said plot to Mirza Golam Hafiz by a deed dated 30-3-1961.  10. It has been submitted by them that in view of the provisions of Rule 42 and 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 the Revenue Officer designated as Settlement Officer is authorized to correct the record-of-rights if fraud is detected in preparation of the same and in the instant cases respondent Nos. 6 and 7 exercising their power vested under those provisions of law had corrected the khatian and thus the High Court Division erred in law in passing the impugned judgments and orders. 

 13. Mr M. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in Civil Appeal No. 234 of 2015, respondent Nos. 1-6 in Civil Appeal No. 235 of 2015, respondent Nos. 1-3 in Civil Appeal No. 237 of 2015 has made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order passed by the High Court Division. He also submits that the appellants have claimed that they had purchased the land in question from the liquidation cell through 5 registered deeds being Deed No.1936 dated 14-7-1988, Deed No.1618 dated 21-6-1988, Deed No.1619 dated 21-6-1988, Deed No.1620 dated 21-6-1988 and Deed No.1621 dated 21-6-1988 respectively and thus, BTMC became the owners, but in Deed No.1936 the disputed land CS plot No.16, SA dag No. 2534, RS dag No.4015 and Mohanagor dag No.4087, of the writ petitioner-respondent No.1 (in CA No. 234 of 2015), has not been mentioned, but the appellants by virtue of official position and force most illegally deleted the name of the writ petitioners and substituted the name of BTMC under the garb of a correction application without support of any rules after final publication of record-of-rights by an official notification dated 10-1-2000 and, as such, the judgment and order of the High Court Division declaring the order 22-8-2007 passed by Charge Officer, Settlement Office, Dhaka to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect, is just and proper. 

 15. The learned Advocate further submits that admittedly no question of fraud was ever been agitated and, as such, in the absence of any allegation of fraud writ respondent No.7 cannot correct the record-of-rights in exercising power under section 42 and 42A of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Rules 1955 and, as such, the order dated 22-8-2007 passed by the writ respondent No. 7 deleting the record-of-rights of the respondent(s) is illegal. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that writ respondent No.7 in his judgment and order dated 22-8-2007 allowed the Settlement Appeal No. 27935 of 2000 along with 32 appeals deleting the record of right of present respondent(s) and substituting the name of the appellant in the said record-of-rights on the ground that ownership of the land has been settled in favour of the BTMC by a judgment passed by the this Division in an appeal, though in the aforesaid Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 390 of 2002 (arising out of writ petition No. 1416 of 1997) the property of respondent No. 1 was not included or the subject matter of the writ petition nor any way relates to the land of present respondent(s) even they or their predecessors were not party in the said writ petition and the findings of the this Division is based on statements of fact hence the said judgments passed by this Division is not binding upon the respondent No.1 and as has been rightly found by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4758 of 2008 and, as such, the judgment of the High Court Division is just, right and proper and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 17. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgments and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 "42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights-The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time the Revenue-officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference." 

 20. It is now well settled by this Division that if fraud has been done or found in recording-of-rights before final publication thereof the Revenue Officer can hear the matter a fresh after consulting the relevant records, making such inquiry necessary, if he deems and can give an opportunity of being heard of the parties. In this connection we can rely on the case of Bhawal Raj of Wards vs Rashida Begum reported in 15 BLC (AD) 115, CA No. 2 of 2004 Government of Bangladesh and others vs Shamsul Hoque and another and CA No. 204 of 2004 Imam Shirajul Hoque and another vs Director-General, Land, Record and survey and others. 

 21. The appellants have failed to show us that the Settlement Authority had made any inquiry that the respondents fraudulently managed to entry their respective names in the record-of-rights as per provision of rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

 23. It has been also argued that the appellant BTMC has failed to prove that in recording the record-of-rights the respondents had committed fraud in preparing the same. 

 24. If we considered these submissions of the learned Advocates for the writ-petitioners-respondents coupled with the above propositions of law, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respondents that repeated rehearing of the appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is not permissible in law. Moreover, it is our considered view that before rehear an appeal under rule 31, the settlement authority had not made any inquiry whether fraud had been committed in recording of rights in the name of respondents. 

 25. Mr M. Qumrul Haque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents in CA Nos. 234, 235 and 239 of 2015 submits that rule 42A provides correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights and in the instant cases the Charge Officer of Settlement office rehear the appeals repeatedly under rule 31 after the final publication of the record-of-rights, which was published in Bangladesh Gazette on January 24,2008. 

 26. The word 'before final publication of record-of-rights,' as mentioned in rule 42A of the Rule 1955 is very important and to deal with the above issue the scheme of law so far as relates to preparation of record-of-rights, as provided in rules 30-35 and 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 are required to be looked, which are as follows: 

 30. Objection—Blank forms of objection shall be supplied free-of-charge, and all objections shall, as far as practicable, be made in such forms, Along with the original objection, the objector shall file a copy or copies of the same for service on all other persons who, in the opinion of the Revenue-officer are materially interested in the case. The Revenue-officer shall issue notices informing the objector and all other persons so interested of the date and place fixed for the hearing of the objection and, with each notice to a person, other than the objector, he shall forward a copy of the objection. Objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue-officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and an abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties materially interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue-officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned. " 

 (2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision." 

 32. Preparation of Final Records—When all objections under rule 30 and all appeals under rule 31 have been disposed of and when the draft record of rights has been corrected in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, the Revenue-officer shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. 

 In cases, however, where operations under Chapter XIV of the Act have been undertaken and fair and equitable rents have been settled and the settlement rent-roll has been finally framed under sub-section (3) of section 109, the Revenue-officer shall, after the draft record-of-rights has been corrected in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, incorporate in the draft record-of-rights the rent determined in respect of each holding or tenancy on the basis of such finally framed settlement rent-roll and then proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. 

 Provided that in a case where the fair and equitable rent have not been so settled and the settlement rent-roll has been finally framed by the time the record-of-rights is ready for final publication, the Revenue-officer instead 

 of withholding final publication of the record-of-rights, may finally frame and finally publish the same noting the existing rents therein without incorporating the fair and equitable rent settled under Chapter XIV of the Act. 

 The final records shall be prepared in conformity with the draft records corrected as above and shall consist of a series of khatians prepared in forms which are generally similar to the forms used for the khatians of the draft record-of-rights. The Khasra shall not form part of the final record-of-rights. The final record shall be printed or prepared in manuscript according to the direction as may be given by the Provincial Government, by general or special order." 

 33. Publication of Final Records —The Revenue-officer shall publish the final record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection, free of charge, during a period of not less than 30 days, at such convenient place as he may determine. A proclamation shall previously be published in each village informing the Maliks and tenants and the Deputy Commissioner of the place at which the final record-of-rights of that village will be open to public inspection and the period during which it will be open to such inspection. 

 34. Certificate of final publication—(1) When a record-of-rights has been finally published under rule 33, the Revenue-officer shall, within sixty days from the date of final publication, make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof and shall date and subscribe the same with his name and official title. 

 (2) The Provincial Government may, by notification, in the official Gazette, declare, with regard to any specified area, that record-of-rights has been finally published for every village included in such area; and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. 

 35. Presumption as to the correctness of record-of-rights—(1) When a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act. 

 (2) Every entry in a record-of-rights finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. 

 42. Special Power of Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer—A Revenue-officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer' may, at any time before the publication of final record-of-rights, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district, or local area, shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. 

 27. Upon perusal of the above rules, it transpires that rule 30 permits filing of `Objection' against any error or mistake appearing in the DP Khatian and requires the Revenue Officer to dispose of the objections after taking evidence. Rule 31 provides for appeal against the decision of the Revenue Officer given under rule 30. A Revenue Officer with additional designation of Settlement Officer is the forum for such appeal. Rule 32 provided that the Revenue Officer is to proceed to frame the 'Final Record-of-Rights,' which is to be 'printed' or 'prepared in manuscript'. 

 28. Rule 33 makes it mandatory for the Revenue Officer to publish final record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection, free of charge, during a period of not less than 30 days, as such convenient place as he may determine. And a proclamation shall previously be published in each village informing the Maliks and tenants and the Deputy Commissioner of the place at which the final record-of-rights of that village will be open to public inspection and the period during which it will be open for such inspection. Rule 34(1) requires that the Revenue Officer, within 60 days of such final publication, to make a certificate stating the fact of 'final publication' and thereof he shall subscribe with date, name and official designation. Sub-rule 2 of rule 34 says that Government may, by notification, in the official Gazettes, declare with regard to any specific area that the record-of-rights has been finally published and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. Rule 35(1) speaks that when a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act. 

 29. In the instant cases from the records, it transpires that final publication of the record-of-rights, as required under Rule 33 was completed and the certificate of final publication as required under Rule 34(1) was also completed vide notification ( প্রজ্ঞাপন) vide নং ভূঃ মঃ/শাঃ-২ (গঃ বিঃ)- ১১/২০০৫-১৬- dated 10-1-2000, though the said notification was published in the Official Gazette on 24-1-2008, which is optional and a mere formality to confer the status of "Conclusive proof" to the final publication. 

 30. In view of the above, we have no hesitation to hold that in the instant cases the settlement authority has proceeded beyond its jurisdiction to rehear the appeals repeatedly in the grab of rule 31 despite the notification ( প্রজ্ঞাপন) vide নং ভূঃ মঃ/শাঃ-২ (গঃ বিঃ)- ১১/২০০৫-১৬ dated 10-1-2000 which was published on 24-1-2008 in official gazette, and it remains unquestionable to testify the fact that, FINAL PUBLICATION under Rule 34 (1) by the 'Revenue Officer' was completed before 10-1-2000. In view of rule 35(1) when a record-of-rights is finally published under rule 33, such publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and rule 35(2) speaks that every entry in a record-of-rights finally published, shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry, and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. Thus, the repeated hearing of appeals under Rule 31 or even under Rule 42 or 42A, by the Revenue Officers after final publication of a record-of-rights is without lawful authority, illegal and is of no legal effect. 

 31. Rule 42A does not give any authority to rehear an appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 by the concerned Settlement Officer after publication of the final record-of-rights, as the such publication is conclusive evidence (rule 35) and thus, in the instant cases the Settlement Officer has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in re-hearing the appeals repeatedly.

 11. Mr. Sk. Md. He again submits that Khatian has no presumptive value as such the impugned judgment and decree shall sustain and the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He lastly submits that the plaintiffs categorically stated in the plaint that: 

 15. it appears that the trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their claim that the condition attached to the kabala dated 09.06.1917 was not complied with by the vendees of the kabala; The kabala dated 05.01.1923 (exhibit-'l ha') shows that Abdul, Azim, Sabu, Asmat and Jasmat together sold 22 bighas and 6.75 kathas of land to Shushila Sundari and thus the CS. recorded tenants Abdul, Azim and Sabu admitted the title of Asmat and Jasmat and therefore the plaintiffs cannot deny the title of the defendants who are the heirs of Shushila Sundari; The kabala dated 09.07.1923 (exhibit- ‘ga,') proves that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs cultivated the suit land as bargadar of Shushila Sundari and thus they admitted the title of the defendant's predecessor-in-interest. Relevant portion of the judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is quoted herein as under: 

 The observation of the lower court that the defendant-respondents could establish their title & possession to the suit jute thus stands on mere conjecture & surmise having no proof of evidence." (Sic) 

 17. Admittedly, the original owners i.e. Aim Uddin Mollah and Abdul Mollah transferred 11 bighas and 17 kathas of land infavour of Asmat Ullah and Jasrnat ullah by registered deed dated 09.06.1917 (exhibit-la') with a condition that the vendees would pay Tk.450/- to the ex-landlord, a debt of the vendors. There is a dispute between the parties regarding the payment and non-payment of the said debt of Tk.450/-. 

 21. Again, defendants claimed that the original owners i.e. Azim Uddin Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Sena Mollah alongwith the purchaser of registered deed dated 09.06.1917 i.e. Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah jointly transferred 22 highs and 6.75 kathas of land infavour of Shushila Shundari Ghosh, predecessor of the defendant nos.67 and 68, vide registered deed dated 05.01.1923. They produced the original copy of deed no.112 dated 05.01.1923 which was marked as exhibit- 'Um'. On perusal of exhibit-‘kha' it appears that said registered deed is an original copy of more than 30 years old document which is sub-mitted in the court by the proper custodian of that deed. 

 22. As per provisions of Section 90 of the Evidence Act there is a presumption infavour of a thirty years old original copy of a registered deed which is submitted in the court from proper custody. For proper appreciation Section 90 of the Evidence Act is reproduced below: 

 23. From the provisions of above mentioned Section of the Evidence Act it appears that the exhibited copy of thirty years old registered document dated 05.01.1923 is being an original copy and produced before the court from proper custody as such the presumption infavour of deed no.112 dated 05.01.1923 is that the said deed is a genuine one. In such a situation the onus of proof of the allegation of the plaintiffs regarding lending money by taking signature in blank stamp and thereafter used the same to create forged document by the predecessor of the defendant nos.67 and 68 lies upon the plaintiffs. 

 26. Again, on perusal of registered deed dated 05.01.1923 (exhibit-Kha) it appears that Abdul, Azim, Sabu, Asmat and Jasmat together sold 22 bighas and 6.75 kathas of Land to Shush la SundAri And thus the original owner Abdul, Azim and Sabu admitted the title of Asmat and Jasmat and therefore the plaintiffs cannot deny the title of the defendants who are the heirs of Shushila Sundari. Moreover, registered deed dated 05.01.1923 executed infavour of Shushila Sundari by the vendors Azim, Abdul, Sabu alongwith Asmat Ullah and Jasmat Ullah (purchaser of the land vide deed dated 09.06.1917) clearly proves that the registered deed dated 09.06.1917 was acted upon on payment of debt of the ex-landlord as per condition of the deed dated 09.06.19.17. Thus, the claim of the plaintiffs that the condition attached to the deed dated 09.06.1917 (exhibit-Ka) was not complied with lies upon the plaintiffs. But the High Court Division without considering legal and factual aspect of the suit arrived at an erroneous decision that the claim regarding noncompliance of the condition of paying debt of Tk.450/- is upon the defendants. 

 30. From the aforementioned discussions, we are of the view that since the suit land was purchased by Shushila Sundari before C.S. operation, the C.S. record should have been prepared in her name. Again, on perusal of exhibit-'neo' i.e. M.R.R. khatian no.15 it appears that said khaitian was prepared in the name of Shushila Sundari in continuation of kabala dated 09.06.1917 and 05.01.1923 which are marked as exhibit-la' and ‘kha' respectively, as such said M.R.R khatian was prepared correctly. From the contents of kabala dated 18.06.1080 (exhibit-'pa') and another kabala also dated 18.06.1980 (exhibit-' fa' it appears that defendant no.69 purchased portion of the suit land from the heirs of Shushila Sundari. Thus Trial Court justly arrived at a finding that plaintiffs have failed to prove their title in the suit land. 

 "It is well-settled that when a finding of fact is based upon the credibility of evidence involving the appreciation of the demeanour of witnesses, the view of the trial court is entitled to great weight and should not be lightly discarded." 

 45. in the present suit plaintiffs hopelessly failed to prove their title as well as possession over the suit land. Since the finding of the trial court is based on proper appreciation of evidence on record, thus the same should not be discarded lightly.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Md. Abu Zafor Siddique

parties:
Abdul Mahn (Md) and others Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioners
Vs
People's Republic of Bangladesh and others----- Defendant-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Zakir Hossain, J: At the instance of the petitioners, this Court was pleased to issue Rule with the following terms: "Records need not be called for. Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 & 2 to show cause as to why the delay of 5549 days in filing this civil revision against the judgment and decree dated 9-7-2007 (decree being drawn on 16-7-2007) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 552 of 2003 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 24-2-2003 (decree being drawn on 3-3-2003) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 437 of 2000 decreeing the suit on contest should not be condoned and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

 2. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule are inter alia that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the Title Suit No. 437 of 2000 before the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and also for declaration that the suit property is not a vested property of the Government. The plaintiffs claimed that 54 acres land from the CS Plot No. 636 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 270 in Mouja Vakurta belonged to Mon Mohon Das and Shema Dashi and SA Khatian was duly prepared in their names. Mon Mohon Das died leaving a son, Behari Lal Das and Shema Dashi died leaving sisters, son Kishore Lal Das and some lands were recorded in the name of Keshob Lal Das. RS Khatian was prepared in the name of Keshob Lal Das. Thereafter Keshob Lal Das sold out 54 decimal lands to Md Moslem Uddin on 1-1-1980 who mutated his name and paid rent to the Government. After that Moslem Uddin sold all their lands to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs being owner have been possessing the said lands peacefully. 

 4. The case of the defendant, in short, is that the suit land was treated as a vested property by virtue of the VP Case No. 70 of 1979. The Government is the custodian of the suit land. The Government leased out the suit land to different persons. The plaintiffs have no right, title and interest over the suit land, therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs. 

 5. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Joint District Judge delving into the evidence on records and considering the legal position involved in this case was pleased to decree the suit by assigning cogent reason. Being aggrieved by and highly dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant-opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 552 of 2003 before the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka. After admitting the appeal, the learned District Judge, Dhaka transmitted the record of the appeal for speedy disposal to the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka without making the appeal ready for hearing. The learned Additional District Judge without waiting for service of summons upon the respondents and without giving notice of transfer to the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners heard the appeal in their absence and allowed the appeal ex-parte by his judgment dated 9-7-2007 and set-aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court without assigning any cogent reason with a stroke of a pen. The plaintiff-petitioners were not at all aware as to the ex-parte decree. It is also contended that the Tadbirkar of the plaintiff-petitioners left this transitory world after passing the decree by the trial Court and by lapse of time, some of the plaintiffs also passed away. The petitioners had no knowledge about the pendency of the appeal after transferring from the Court of the learned District Judge to the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka. It is further contended that the petitioners were not aware of the ex-parte judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court. It is further contended that the petitioners being in possession of the suit land got some threats of eviction from some miscreants on 5-6-2022 and 28-6-2022. The miscreants published that they got lease from the Government. Thereafter, the petitioners were aware as to the judgment of the Appellate Court from the office of the respondent Government. It is also mentioned that the petitioners with their might and main tried their level best to contact their appointed lawyer and they did not find his address to communicate. Thereafter, the petitioners engaged a new lawyer and after incurring huge time managed to obtain the certified copy of the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The respondents are powerful man in the locality and they are using political and monetary power to dispossess the petitioners. Finding no other alternative, the petitioners were constrained to prefer the aforesaid revisional application with a petition for condonation of delay. After hearing the same, the Court was pleased to issue the aforesaid Rule. 

 7. She further submits that the petitioners being in possession of the suit land got some threats of eviction from some miscreants on 5-6-2022 and 28-6-2022. The miscreants told that the Government leased out the suit land in their favour, thereafter, the petitioners went to the office of the respondents wherefrom the petitioners got to know about the judgment of the Appellate Court and subsequently, the petitioners tried a lot to contact their earlier lawyer but found no trace of him. Then the petitioners engaged a new lawyer who tried her level best to collect the certified copy of the relevant records but failed to trace the record for a couple of months. It took a lot only to find out the original record of the Court. 

 8. The learned Advocate further submits that against the decree, the defendant-appellant-opposite parties on 1-12-2003 filed appeal being Title Appeal No. 552 of 2003 causing delay of 242 days. The appellant submitted Court-fees on 18-2-2004. The order for serving notice upon the parties was passed on 1-4-2004. It appears from Order No. 12 dated 8-5-2004 that notice upon the respondents Nos. 1-3, 5-6 returns after service as per the report of the process server, the respondents No. 6 appeared with a power and filed hazira, notice upon the respondents Nos. 4, 7-10 had not been returned, after service. On 7-6-2004, the notice upon the respondents Nos. 8 and 10 returned after service notice upon them, the notice upon the respondents Nos. 7 and 9 returned unserved and only respondent Nos. 5-7 appeared by power and no one for the appellant appeared. In this order, there is no mention as to whether the notice upon the respondent No. 4 was served or not. However, from the Order No. 14 dated 24-7-2004, it appears that the notice upon the respondent No. 4 returned unserved, and respondent Nos. 1-2 and 8-10 appeared by power and filed hazira, and on the other hand, respondent Nos. 5 and 7 filed time petition for filing written statement and there was no step on the part of the appellant. She contends that very surprisingly on the following date i.e. on 7-9-2004, the Appellate Court mentioned that "respondent filed hazira, no step was taken by the appellant upon the respondent No. 4 to 6-10-2004 for taking steps." Therefore, it is clear that no notice was served upon the respondent No. 4 and the respondent No. 3 did not appear before the Court. On the next date i.e. on 6-10-2004, it appears from Order No. 16 that the respondent filed hazira and the appellant took no step but on the same date, the Appellate Court suo motu condoned the delay and admitted the appeal and also called for the LCR without any appearance or step of the defendant-appellants. Therefore, it appears from the order that though the appellant took no step but in absence of the appellant and in presence of the learned Advocate for the respondent, the appeal was admitted by condoning the delay of 242 days by which necessarily indicates vicious and malafide connivance between the appellant and the learned advocate of the respondents. 

 9. The learned Advocate further submits that the law does not allow an appeal to be admitted when there was none to place the appeal before the Court; specially an appeal filed out of time should not be registered and admitted without deciding whether the appellants are entitled to the condonation of delay. In absence of the appellants, the Appellate Court can only dismiss the appeal for default and there is no scope for the Appellate Court to condone delay at its own motion when there was none for the appellant to get the application for condonation of delay heard before the Appellate Court. The learned Advocate also made submission regarding the connivance of the earlier Advocates who acted against the interest of the petitioners. The learned Advocate further added that the present revision, if the Rule is issued upon condonation of delay as per the satisfaction of this Court, involves an important question of law which has already been settled by our Apex Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2310 of 2018 (Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Hye and others) that "this Division declared all actions, decisions regarding listing any property as vested property after 23-3-1974 as illegal." In the present case, the defendant-appellant-opposite party Government claimed over the suit land by way of a VP Case being No. 69 of 1978; therefore in view of the aforesaid provision of law, the claim of the Government is not tenable in eye of law. 

 "1 have perused the record but I do not find any original deed of the plaintiff. On the perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiff sides have withdrawn all the deeds but they did not re-file. Plaintiff side could not prove their possession over the suit land. They also could not prove their title over the suit land by filing the original deed." 

 "The trial Court dismissed the suit at the first instance. On appeal the decision was set-aside and the case sent back on remand for fresh trial. After the arrival of the records while the suit was lying pending for disposal in the First Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal the learned District Judge, by an order dated 15 July 1992, transferred the suit from the said Court to the second Additional Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal for disposal. There was no appearance of the contesting defendant before the transferee Court. As a result the learned Assistant Judge, Second Additional Court heard the matter ex-parte but dismissed the suit on 30 August 1992. The plaintiff took an appeal; Title Appeal No. 195 of 1992 therefrom. The appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat who reversed the decision of the trial Court and decreed the suit on 8 November 1993. Being aggrieved defendant No. 1 preferred Civil Revision No. 221 of 1994. A Single Bench of the High Court Division set-aside the decree of the Appellate Court on the view that the defendant was not informed of the transfer of the suit from the First Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal to the Second Additional Court, Barisal as required under section 24A(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for which he could not defend his cause in the case. Accordingly, the learned Judge sent back the case on remand to the trial Court for disposal by his judgment and order dated 24 February 1997." 

 vii. If the delay is not condoned, meritorious case may be thrown to the street and the alleged lessees shall grasp the property without any valid title.

parties:
Tania Rahman ------- Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works and others -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
5. The petitioner's case inter alia is that the Hon'ble Prime Minister instructed the RAJUK to allot plot to the titled freedom fighters and accordingly the RAJUK invited applications in the national newspapers on 26-11-2008, for allotting land/plot in Uttara 3rd Phase Extension Project Residential Model Town. The respondent No. 8. being a veteran freedom fighter, made an application 13-1-2009 to the respondent No. 2 for getting an allotment of land in said residential Model Town of RAJUK. That the respondent No. 2 approved the application of the respondent No. 8 and issued a provisional allotment letter in favour of respondent No. 8 in the category of "Freedom Fighter" vide Memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE-2/621 Stha; dated 25-1-2011. That following receipt of the provisional allotment letter, the respondent No. 8 appointed Md Mojibur Rahman as his attorney for management of, and transfer of, the scheduled land by way of registered power of attorney deed No. 6169 dated 16-5-2011. That subsequently after receipt of payment of the 1st installment for the plot on 31-7-2011, the respondent No. 2 issued a final allotment letter of the scheduled land (plot ID No. 15C1-4-5) vide Memo No. RAJUK/Estate-2/515 Stha: dated 3-11-2011 in favour of the respondent No. 8 subject to the payment of 2nd and 3rd installments amounting to Taka 8,10,000 in total. That the respondent No. 8 paid the 2nd and 3rd installments for the scheduled land within 29-12-2011 as required under the final allotment letter. That following receipt of the requisite payment, the respondent No. 2 and respondent No. 8 executed a lease agreement on 12-11-2012 and lease the scheduled land in favour of respondent No. 8 for a period of 99 (ninety nine) years with effect from 3-11-2011 with the terms and conditions contained in the said lease agreement which was finally executed by way of Registered Deed No. 1156 dated 30-1-2013. Later, the physical possession of the plot was handed over to the respondent No. 8 by the RAJUK and the scheduled land was also mutated in the name of Respondent No. 8. That by way of application dated 7-5-2013, the respondent No. 8 through his constituted attorney, Md Mojibur Rahman, approached the respondent No. 6' for transfer of the allotted land in favour of the petitioner. That the respondent No. 2 through its Assistant Director (Estate-2) Zonal Office, Uttara, Dhaka asked to deposit the requisite transfer fees of Taka 2.16,000 (Two lac and sixteen thousand only) in total within a period of 1(one) month for the transfer of the scheduled plot in favour of the petitioner vide Memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE-2/UTTARA (3rd Parbo)/1398 Stha: dated 17-6-2013. That according to instructions of above memo issued by the respondent No. 2, the respondent No. 8 through his constituted attorney deposited the said amount in the account of RAJUK. Subsequently, the Respondent No. 2 vide a letter of permission dated 17-6-2013 permitted the respondent No. 8 to transfer the scheduled land/plot by way of registration in favour of the petitioner. That following permission from RAJUK, the respondent No. 8 through its constituted attorney executed a registered sale deed in favour of the petitioner vide registered sale deed No. 7210 dated 26-6-2013 and delivered the possession of the scheduled land to the petitioner thereof. That thereafter, the petitioner made an application to the respondent No. 6 for mutation of the scheduled land in her name and attached the certified copy of the registered sale of deed. That later, as per instructions of the respondent No. 2 contained in Memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE-2/UTTARA (3rd Parbo)/1808 Stha: dated 31-7-2013, the petitioner deposited the required amount for mutation charge and the respondent No. 2 recorded and mutated the scheduled land in the name of the petitioner vide memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE/UTTARA (3rd Parbo)/1932 Stha: dated 22-8-2013 issued under the signature of respondent No. 9. Further, by the said memo, the respondent No. 2 deems the petitioner as the lessee of the scheduled land/plot since then. That since the execution of sale deed and mutation of the land in favour of the petitioner in 2013, the petitioner have been enjoying the leasehold title and possession of the scheduled land by paying Land Development Taxs (paid up to Bangla year 1429). That suddenly on 16-2-2016 the office of the respondent No. 6 asked the original allotee, the respondent No. 8 and the existing lessee, the petitioner to appear before the Director (Estate and Lease-1), RAJUK on 25-2-2016 with all the necessary documents with regard to two plots (plot No. 5 plot No. 22) of Uttara (3rd Phase) Extended Project. That the petitioner being unaware of the reasons for calling her before the RAJUK, went to the office of the Respondent No. 6 on the date fixed and came to learn that the respondent No. 8 earlier applied for getting allotment of a plot in the Uttara (3rd Phase) Extended project of RAJUK Model Town and was allotted one being Plot No. 22 of Road No. 1/A. In the year 2011 he made another application for allotment of land by concealing the earlier allotment and got the plot in question Plot No. 5 at Road No. 4 (scheduled land). Hence the respondent No. 6 asked all concerned with regard to those two plots to attend before this office. That during hearing at the office of the respondent No. 6 on 25-2-2016, the petitioner made statements in support of her right, title and possession of the schedule land by dint of registered sale deed Registered Sale Deed No. 7210 dated 26-6-2013 and mutation documents. She also confirms that she had no knowledge or issue with the earlier allotment as a bonefide purchaser on permission. 

 That the respondent No. 8 appeared and made a written statement contending, inter alia, that he is not at all aware of the fate of the earlier application and the allotment. He deposited no premium against the alleged allotment: it must have been resorting to frauds and may be with the assistance of the RAJUK officials. He further requested to cancel the previous allotment and maintain the latter one. That subsequently on a number of occasions, the petitioner visited the office of the respondent No. 6 and she was assured that her plot would not be affected since title and possession had already passed to her validly from the respondent No. 8. That all on a sudden on 9-3-2020 by way of Memo No. RAJUK/ESTATE and land-2/UTTARA/562 Stha, the respondent No. 6 cancelled allotment of the scheduled land, originally issued in faovur of the respondent No. 8 and confiscated all the money received by RAJUK in relation to the said land. By the same memo, the respondent No. 6 maintained allotment of the Plot No. 22 of Road No. 1/A in favour of the respondent No. 8 and notified him about the decision of lst/2020 meeting of the authority. However, the petitioner being the lessee did not receive any letter of cancellation of their lease/mutation. Nor did she receive any letter from RAJUK notifying her of the cancellation of the said allotment. Hence the petitioner being aggrieved filed the instant writ petition. 

 7. Learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the impugned cancellation of allotment of the plot by the respondents is absolutely without lawful authority and is of no legal effect: He submits that the petitioner Tania Rahman by way of purchase from the original lessee Captain (Retd) Md Abdul Hai, Bir Protik who is the respondent No. 8 in the writ petition has been accorded all the rights of a lessee. He continues that therefore cancellation of the plot without affording due process to the petitioner herself is not sustainable and is a violation of the fundamental rights of the petitioner Guaranteed under the Constitution. He contends that it is admitted by the respondents that the respondent No. 8, Captain (Retd) Md Abdul Hai, Bir Protik the original lessee transferred the plot with the permission of the respondent No. 2 and which is evident from the materials placed before the Bench. He contends that therefore totally ignoring the petitioner in not acknowledging her as the present lawful lessee is not acceptable and is violative of the laws and rules including the provisions of the Constitution. 

 8. In support of his submissions he draws our attention to Annexure-L, L1 and L2 and  sub-sequently Annexure-M of the writ petition. He particularly draws our attention to Annexure-L1 of the writ petition dated 22-8-2013 issued by the office of the respondent No.2. He points out that in clear language used in Annexure- L1 it is manifest that the plot was transferred with the permission of the Respondents including doing recording, mutation in the petitioner's name. He continues that the clear language of Annexure L1 shows that the respondents acknowledge the petitioner as an independent lessee pursuant to transfer of the property from the respondent No. 8 Captain (Retd) Md Abdul Hai, Bir Protik who is the original lessee. He particularly draws attention to the sentence “এখন হইতে আপনাকে উক্ত প্লটের হস্তান্তর সূত্রে লীজ গ্রহিতা/গ্রহিত্রী হিসাবে গণ্য করা হইবে।” On this issue he continues that therefore the respondent No. 2 clearly acknowledged the petitioner as a lessee in her own right by way of transfer and the respondents cannot now derogate from their own words and actions. He contends that therefore issuing the impugned order in the name of the original lessee and not in the name of the petitioner is totally upon misapplication of mind of the respondents given that the original lessee meanwhile extinguished all his right back in 2013 and admittedly with the permission of the respondents. He submits that therefore not affording due process to the petitioner is an aberration from the principle of due process which the respondents cannot lawfully sustain. 

 10. Next he makes submissions on the primary allegation of the respondents the original lessee having deceived the respondents subsequently was allotted two plots. He denies these allegations and submits that the original lessee respondent No. 8 was not at all aware that he was also originally allotted an earlier plot being plot No. 22 in sector 4 of Uttara. Upon another query from this bench he asserts that the petitioner is a bonafide purchaser and was not at all aware of the circumstances of any plot being allotted in the original lessees's name. He submits that it is evident from the materials that the RAJUK in 2013 having full knowledge of all the circumstances including that the petitioner have been transferred the property by the original lessee consciously granted the permission to transfer. 

 12. We drew the petitioner to the clear mandate of the Rules of the Dhaka Improvement Trust (Allotment of Lands) Rules 1969. The learned Advocate for the petitioner argued that it is clear from the documents that the respondent No. 8 transferred the property to the present lessee with the permission of the Respondents in the year 2013 with full knowledge of RAJUK. He submits that it is clear from the documents that the petitioner has been transferred the property by the Respondent No.8 Bir Protik through out the procedure with knowledge and permission of the respondent No. 2, RAJUK with all proper documents. He submits that it is also manifest from the documents that the cancelled plot was allotted in the name of the original lessee in the year 2011 and purchased the plot in 25-1-2011. Subsequently lease-deed registration was done in 2012 pursuant to which in 2013 the land was transferred to the present lessee. He submits that it is absurd to hold that in the span of 2 years the respondents could not discover that the lessor was allotted a plot if at all he was ever lawfully allotted a plot previously. He submits that it was the respondents duty to exercise their due diligence before granting permission to transfer the land in the name of the present lessee petitioner. In support of his submissions he draws attention to clause No. 6 of Annexure-Y-21 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 2. From Annexure-Y-21 he particularly draws attention to clause 6 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition. Clause 6 of the Annexure-Y-21 is reproduced below: 

 13. He asserts that therefore it is clearly stated by the respondents themselves that only after being satisfied as to the regularity of allotment of plots can the respondents accepted the second installment. He submits that it is evident that in this case the respondents accepted and received all the installments and the plot was transferred duly after exhausting all the procedures including permission from the Respondents. He assails that therefore the respondents cannot now go back on their conduct and claim that the allotment of plot was not regular on the plea that the original lessee was already allotted one plot earlier. He further submits that there are no laches on the part of the petitioner and moreover the petitioner is an independent lessee by virtue of the lease-deed and the respondents are bound by the terms of such lease-deed. He re-asserts that by way of Annexure-L1 the respondents have accepted the petitioner as an independent and new lessee and the respondents have themselves acknowledged all the terms of the original lease-deed between the original lessee and lessor which shall be applicable to the present lessee and which shall be considered as a fresh lease-deed. On the issue of the lease-deed which is Annexure-F to be considered as a fresh lease-deed, he submits that on the one hand the lessee is a fresh lessee and the lease-deed is a fresh lease-deed while on the other hand it is clear that the present petitioner was never allotted any plot in her name by the RAJUK. He contends that the present petitioner duly abided by clause 9 and 10 of the Dhaka Improvement Trust (Allotment of Lands) Rules 1969 given that the present petitioner never made any misstatement regarding her position since it is clear that she never applied for any other plot besides the present plot. He argues that therefore it would be reasonable to hold that the petitioner been acknowledged by the Respondents as a fresh lessee particularly by way of Annexure-L1 flier alia other documents and also the fact that the lease-deed shall be considered as a fresh lease-deed which is stated by the respondents themselves and further given the fact that the petitioner never applied for any land therefore she ought to be afforded the process she is entitled to under the law as a lawful lessee. He further asserts that the respondents committed a fundamental mistake in still holding the original lessee as the allotte of the cancelled plot. He continues that whereas it is clear that the respondents by their own document and their own action transferred the whole interest of the plot in the name of the petitioner with all the rights and liabilities arising out of the lease-deed. 

 14. There was a query from this bench upon the petitioner as to when the right and liability of the original lessee was transferred to the present petitioner present lessee, should such transfer of duties and liabilities also involve the liabilities of the original lessee as far as the liability of misrepresentation of facts regarding the dispute over the number of allotment of the plots is concerned. In reply he contends that in accordance with annexure-LI of the writ petition which is issued by the respondent No. 2 read along with some other documents the petitioner and the respondents are only bound to each other within the terms of the lease-deed which is Annexure-F of the writ petition. He draws our attention to the lease-deed which is Annexure-F of the writ petition. He particularly takes us to clause 26 and 29 of the writ petition Clause 26 and 29 is reproduced below: 

 found to have been made falsely or by way of suppression or distortion of material, facts than notwithstanding the fact that the Lease Deed has already been registered or that the possession of the demised property has been delivered to the LESSE of that the construction has been registered or that the possession of the demised property has been delivered to the LESSEE of that the construction has been registered or that the possession of the demised property has been delivered to the LESSEE or that the construction has been made, the LESSOR shall be entitled to cancel the allotment, determine the lease in accordance with the provision of Clause 29(1) hereinafter and forfeit the premium paid by the LESSEE and on such determination, the demised property and any construction thereon shall vest in the LESSOR and be the absolute property f the LESSOR free from all encumbrances. 

 (i) In the event of the LESSEE committing breach of any of the covenants of this Indenture other than payment of rent and taxes and there being no specific provisions in respect of such breach in this covenant the LESSOR shall be at liberty without prejudice to any other rights that it any possess, after giving one calendar month's notice in writing, to determine the lease under these presents. re-enter into or upon the whole of the demised property or any part thereof and take possession thereof including all buildings, structures etc. thereon and thereupon the lease shall forthwith cease and the demised property including all buildings, structures etc. thereon shall wholly vest in and be the absolute property of the LESSOR but the LESSEE shall be entitled only to such a compensation for the buildings, structures etc. as many be determined by the Chairman of the Kartripakkha, the Rajdhani Unnayan Dartripakka. The SESSEE, however may remove any goods or things not being part of any building or structure on the demised property within a fortnight of such determination, failing which they shall all be forfeited to the LESSOR and the LESSEE shall not be entitled to any price, compensation or damage whatsoever therefore. 

 16. Taking us through these clauses he submits that these clauses presuppose that even if there is an allegation of suppression of facts or materials infer cilia other material factor whatsoever, it is manifest that a notice under clause 29 must be given to the lessee. He points out that however it is clear that in this case no such notice was issued under clause 29 upon the petitioner prior to cancelling the said plot. He particularly draws attention to clause 26 wherefrom he points out that clause 26 clearly contemplate that in case of any irregularity or suppression of facts by the allottee the procedure in accordance with the provision of clause 29(1) of the lease-deed shall be mandatorily exhausted. He submits that clause No. 26 clearly presupposes that the procedure under clause 29 is to be mandatorily exhausted in the face of allegation of suppression of facts or any other material factor. He assails that in this case it is admitted by the respondents that no such notice under clause 29 was issued upon the petitioner. He submits that therefore the respondents themselves violated the terms of the lease-deed which terms they are duty bound to follow law and rules and that may be relevant for the purpose. He reiterates that the petitioner is a bona fide lessee and therefore the cancellation of the plot which is lawfully alloted in the petitioners name is without lawful authority. He further submits that the petitioner as a 'new' and 'independent' lessee of RAJUK is entitled to have a 'notice to quit' served upon her under clause 29(i) of the original lease-deed dated 30-1-2013 (Annexure-F). He argues that since no such notice has been issued ever consequently the impugned order becomes a product of illegality. He also submits that the RAJUK has no authority to take over/re-enter the property of the petitioner without cancelling the lease of the petitioner and, as such, RAJUK acted illegally, arbitrarily and with malice. He asserts that any false statement, suppression of facts etc. by the respondent No. 8 at the time of making his application for allotment of plot No. 5 is an issue between the lessor (RAJUK) and the previous lessee (respondent No. 8)) and is not applicable at all to the present lessee. He contends that since the plot has been freshly leased out to the petitioner by the lessor RAJUK, the new lessee/petitioner cannot be blamed for no fault of her own. He concludes his submission upon assertion that the Rule bears merit ought to be made absolute for ends of justice. 

 17. On the other hand learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 by way of affidavit-in-opposition followed by two other supplementary affidavit vehemently opposes the Rule. He submits that the original allottee, predecessor of the petitioner admitted that before acquiring 'plot in case' he filed application for a plot, deposited money to RAJUK and thereafter became aware of that he has got a plot and admitted fact need not be proved. And conversely, the Dhaka Improvement Trust (Allotments of Lands) Rules, 1969 as Gazetted in the Dhaka Gazette, part-1, dated the 15th January, 1970 debar any person, his wife/husband, dependent children or other dependent to acquire any plot other than allotted one which is contemplated in rule 9 of the Dhaka Improvement Trust (Allotments of Lands ) Rules, 1969.
