 20. Another aspect is that it is well settled that the certificate of sale does not, by itself, create the title but is merely evidence of title. In the case of Ahmedabad Municipality Vs. Hazi Abdul reported in AIR 1971 SC 1201 it was observed by the Supreme Court of India that it is axiomatic that the purchaser at auction sale takes the property subject to all the defects of title and the doctrine caveat emptor (let the purchaser beware) applies to such purchaser. It is the "right, title and interest" of the judgment-debtor with all risk and defect and without any warranty of title either by the decree-holder or by the court that passes to a purchaser at a court sale, with the exception that where it is proved that the judgment-debtor had no saleable interest at all the purchaser may recover back the purchase-money. In this case, the alleged auction was held on 20.06.1953 showing Khiroda Sundari Saha and Lalit Mohon Saha as certificate debtors. But we have already found from C.S. Khatian (ext-1) shows that Khiroda Sundari Dashya was only C.S. recorded tenant and before holding auction she sold her rayoti interest to Salimunnessa on 27.03.1953 who was not impleaded in the certificate procedure. That is, Khiroda had no right and title at the time of holding auction in suit property so the auction purchaser had not acquired any title because, at the time of holding auction the certificate debtor had no title in the property, in question. It is not the case of the plaintiffs that Salimunnessa had notice of the alleged charges brought by R.L. Acquired Government Estate either actual or constructive. It is to be relevant here to reiterating that in Title Suit No.221 of 1964, the learned Munsif observed that Khiroda and Lalit Mohon were the certificate debtors who already sold their interest to Salimunessa with the knowledge of the defendant No.1, that is, predecessor of the present plaintiffs. Lalit Mohan and Khiroda had no subsisting interest on the date of holding auction sale and it cannot be said that the defendant No.1 (predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs) acquired 7 annas interest by his purchase in the certificate sale. That judgment was upheld in Second Appeal No. 1095 of 1966. That finding is binding upon the plaintiffs. The effect of a sale under the PDR Act being to pass to the purchaser merely the right, title and interest of the person named as judgment debtor in the certificate, the purchaser acquires no right if the person appears to have i no interest in the property at the date of sale. That is, auction purchaser Ali Ahmed did not get any title under it. In Title Suit No.221 of 1964, Title Appeal No.50 1966 and Second Appeal No.1 095 of 1966, the respective Courts had taken notice of the same. But the plaintiffs did not meet up the issue raised and explain the consequences of the same.

 (XVII) The plaintiffs had been in uninterrupted possession of the suit property since their predecessor's time for more than 60 years and if anyone had purchased the suit property, then the said persons are to file suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and not the plaintiffs. 

 34. We have examined the judgment of the trial Court dated 31.03.2004 passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994, the judgment and decree dated 12th and 13th day of May, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 181 of 2004, the judgment and order dated 06.05.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in CPLA No. 1359 of 2009, sale Certificate No. 660 of 1952-53 (exhibit-2), certificate of delivery of possession (exhibit-2(ka), Dhaka Gazette Extra-ordinary published by the authority on April 2, 1956, Gazette Extra-ordinary dated 12.02.1954 and the judgment and decree passed by various Courts in various suits, appeals, etc. and the connected materials on record. 

 35. From the judgment of trial Court in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 decreeing the suit and the judgment of First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 passed by the High Court Division dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that the trial Court and High Court Division by elaborate and threadbare discussions on all the issues involved in the suit filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2-plaintiffs decided merits on the issues on the basis of evidence on record. Both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiff-appellants could prove their title to and possession in the suit property till they were forcibly dispossessed by the defendants. The courts also disbelieved the defendant-appellants case. The CPLA was also dismissed by this Division with reasoning on merit. 

 39. We have examined original sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession as placed before us by Mr. Farooqui at the time of hearing. 

 42. We are of the considered opinion that R.L. (Rup Lal) Court of Wards Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of Tauzi No. 61/1, which is a part of original Tauzi No. 61, of Sahar Dhaka of the Collectorate of Zilla-Dacca. It transpires from the C.S Khatian that it is written therein that Khiroda Shundari Daishya was in possession of No. 1, Atash Khana Lane of Mouza Sahar Dhaka of Khatian No. 241. This clearly shows that the words "Sahar Dhaka" as used in the auction sale certificate was the Mouza of the property sold in auction and the word “মৌজে আতস খানা” does not mean Mouza but it was the lane i.e. Mash Khana Lane. Further, from the deed of sale (Exbt-Ka) submitted by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 (appellants) it appears that the Police Station of the suit property has been stated therein as Kotwali at Present P.S.- Lalbag being premises No. 1, Atash Khana Lane, Dhaka. Thus it is evident that C.S. Khatian No. 241 was originally under P.S. Kotwali but subsequently it fell within P.S. Lalbag. Further, we searched the Gazette of establishment of Lalbag Police Station and finally it was found from the Culcutta Gazette, September 22, 19 45 that: 

 58. Thus, we do not find Exhibit 2 and 2(ka) are forged documents rather, on perusal of the documents it appears to us that these documents are original/genuine documents. 

 59. Moreover, admittedly the plaintiffs' predecessor in interest Doctor Monjurul Hoque @ Ali Ahmed had been in possession of the suit property by virtue of those documents as the defendants failed to prove monthly tenancy of Ali Ahmed or his wife under Khiroda Shundari Daishya or anyone else. Admittedly, the plaintiffs had also been in possession of the suit property, till they were dispossessed during the pendency of the suit. Possession follows title. 

 67. The proposition of law enunciated in the said decision can hardly be disputed. But in the instant case both the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court (High Court Division) considering the documents and all the facts and circumstances of the suit/appeal decided it in favour of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division on examination of the documents held as under: "We have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or non-compliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate or voidable. We are of the view of that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus, to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property." 

 69. On the other hand, this Division in the case of Joynal Abedin and others vs. Mafizur Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 162 held as under: "It appears that the kabuliyats Ext.D series were filed before the trial Court and those were not wrongly marked as exhibits. Consequently, at an earlier point of time the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division remanded the case to the lower appellate Court and those were marked exhibits without any objection by the parties. From the order of the lower appellate Court dated 09.06.83, it appears that those documents were filed by the defendants as per Firisti with a petition for accepting those in evidence and those were admitted in evidence without any objection from either side. Thereafter the appeal was heard in 1985 and in disposing of the appeal we find that the lower appellate Court did not say a word with regard to these kabuliyats nor had taken those into consideration. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division also on an erroneous view of the law left these vital documents out of consideration by holding that the certified copies of the kabuliyats were filed without calling for the original copies of the kabuliyats. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on a worng consideration of section 66 of the Evidence Act left those out of consideration as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was of the opinion that those documents were not admissible in evidence as the originals were not called for. Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants rightly argued that the documents having been filed and marked Exhibit without any objection the question of admissibility of those documents cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time and the courts below including the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not considering these kabuliyats Ext. D series and failed to consider the effect of these kabuliyats in the instant case: The learned Advocate in support of his argument has also cited the case of Abdullah and 3 others Vs. Abdul Karim and others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205. In that decision it has been held that objection as to formal proof of a document is to be taken at the earliest point of time. In the present case, the document was admitted in evidence without any objection from either side in the year 1983. As a matter of fact the appeal came up for hearing in 1985 after a lapse of 2 years. Nobody raised the question of formal proof of those kabuliyats and those were admitted in evidence without objection. This being the position, the kabuliyats, exhibit D series were admissible in evidence and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not considering those kabuliyats. 

 73. We have already seen that in fact the Rup Lal Government Acquired Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of the Tauzi and out of it .568 ajutangsha of land was sold in auction. Moreover, the plaintiffs were admittedly in possession of the suit property. Therefore, if any one claims title to or ownership of the same or part of it, they shall have to file a suit for declaration of title, partition and possession. The defendants, under no circumstance were entitled to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property.

2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that: the present respondent Nos.1-6 as the writ petitioners preferred the Writ Petition No.10627 of 2012 under article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh before the High Court Division for direction upon the respondents to release the 0.75 acres out of 1.50 acres of land proposed to acquire under LA Case No.4/77-78 vide notice of acquisition dated 12-12-1978 which were requisitioned vide notice dated 29-6-1978 issued under sections 5(1a) and 3, respectively, under the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (Act XIII of 1948) (Hereinafter to be referred as the Requisition of Property Act) by the writ respondent No.3 appertaining to SA Khatian No.2128, SA Dag No.1141, JL No.56 under Mouza-Rupatali, Police Station-Kotwali, District-Barisal to the writ petitioners upon reimbursing the Government to the extent actually paid as compensation to the writ petitioners' predecessor at the time of acquisition. It is stated that 1.50 acres of land under Mouja-Rupatali, Police Station-Kotwali, JL No.56, District-Barisal being SA Khatian No.2128, SA Plot No.1141 was acquired under the Requisition of Property Act by the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal (the writ respondent No.3) for requiring body the Roads and Highway Department under the Ministry of Commu-nication for extension of Barishal Highways which originally belonged to Dr Anwar Hossain, who was the full brother of the writ petitioners. Dr Anwar Hossain died leaving behind the writ petitioners, as legal heirs, who applied to the Ministry of land on 22-4-2001 (Annexure-B to the writ petition) for releasing the unused land in favour of the writ petitioners upon which the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal was asked by the Ministry, vide letter dated 30-5-2001 (Annexure-C to the writ petition) to give a report. The Roads and Highway Department, Barishal upon proper inquiry also found that 0.75 acres land out of total acquired 1.50 acres of land is totally unused by the requiring body. The requiring body, Roads and Highway Department vide Memo dated 10-9-2001 and 8-12-2001 (Annexure-D and D(1) to the writ petition) made a recommendation to release the unused 0.75 acre land. and in view of that recommendation Ministry of Communication vide letter dated 11-4-2005 (Annexure-E to the writ petition) gave no objection and consented to release the unused land to the original owners on condition to refund the compensation money as earlier paid to the title holder to the account of Roads and Highway Department. In pursuant to the said letter dated 11-4-2005 (Annexure-E to the writ petition) the Ministry of Land vide letter dated 27-7-2006 (Annexure-F to the writ petition) requested writ respondent No.3, i.e., the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal to submits a report mentioning 4 (four) terms in the said letter pursuant to which the writ respondent No.3, the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal, vide letter dated 29-9-2009 informed the Secretary, Ministry of Land that 1.50 acres of land under SA Plot No. 1141 was acquired vide LA Case No.4/77- 78 and in respect of the said land final Gazette has not yet been published under section 5(7) of the Requisition of Property Act and 0.75 acre of land was lying unused to the requiring body, the Roads and Highway Department. Finally the writ respondent No.3 in the said letter recommended that as the price of the land now has already been increased the writ petitioners' application can be considered if compensation money repaid at the present value of the land. The writ petitioners although applied to the writ respondent No.3 to release and hand over the unused land as per direction of Ministry to the writ petitioners but got no reply. Therefore, the writ petitioners served legal notice upon the writ respondents demanding justice but in vain. The writ petitioners finding no other alternative efficacious remedy moved the above mentioned writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi. 

 6. Mr Goutom Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the lands having been acquired vide LA Case No.4/1977-78 from the title holder Dr. Anwar Hossain for expansion of Highways of Barishal and proper compensation having been paid there is no scope to release the acquired lands and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute and directing the respondents to release the land and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. He further submits that serious disputed question of facts relating to payment of compensation at the earlier rate or present market value of the land of the immovable properties having been involved the High Court Division erred in law in entertaining the writ-petition and making the Rule absolute silting in special statutory jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

 7. Per contra, Mr Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos.1-6 submits that the authority on the recommendation of the requiring body has jurisdiction to release unused acquired land on refund of compensation which was paid to the awardee at the time of acquiring and, as such, the High Court Division rightly passed the impugned judgment. He further submits that the requiring body on an inquiry found that 0.75 acre of land still has been laying as unused and, as such, made the recommendation to release the same in favour of the writ petitioners (herein respondents) as the legal heirs of the original owner. He finally submits that no gazette notification has yet been published finally complying the provision of sub-section (7) of section 5 of the Requisition of Property Act in respect of the land to be acquired. Therefore, acquisition has not yet been completed under the Requisition of Property Act and, as such, there is no legal bar to release the land in question, hence, the High Court Division has rightly passed the impugned judgment directing to release the property. Therefore, on above backdrops the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Hon'ble Division. 

 9. On perusal the averment of the appeal it reveals that 1.50 acres of land under Mouza Rupatali, Police Station: Kotwali, JL No.56, District: Barishal appertaining to SA Khatian No.2128, SA Plot No.1141 was acquired from its owner and possessor vide LA Case No.4 of 1977-78 under the Requisition of Property Act by the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal as respondent No.3 for requiring body Roads and Highway Department under the Ministry of Communication for expansion of Barishal Highways. The writ respondents (herein) as legal heirs of the owner as petitioners filed an application on 3-4-2000 (Annexure-B) to the Ministry of Land for releasing unused land in favour of them. The Ministry of Land vide letter dated 30-5-2001 (Annexure-C) asked the Deputy Commissioner, Barishal (respondent No.3) to give a report after proper inquiry. The Roads and Highway Department, Barishal was asked to submit a report to the respondent No.3, Deputy Commissioner, after proper inquiry. Thereafter, the Executive Engineer Roads and Highway Department, Barishal Division vide Memo dated 20-9-2004 and 8-12-2004 (Annexure-D and D-1) made recommendation to release unused 0.75 acre of land out of 1.50 acres of acquired land. In pursuance of the above memos the Ministry of Communication issued no objection letter vide memo dated 11-4-2005 (Annexure-E) with condition on refund the compensation money as earlier paid to the title holder. 

 11. In view of the claim of the present market value of the land by the respondent No.3 vide letter dated 24-9-2009, the writ petitioners (herein respondents) served a legal notice to the respondents demanding justice, however, in vain. Therefore, the writ petitioner filed the writ petition before the High Court Division praying for the release of the land and direction upon the writ respondents to accept the refund of the compensation at the rate of compensation as earlier paid to the original owner but not as per present value of the land. 

 12. The High Court Division vide its judgment and order dated 20-2-2014 made the Rule absolute directing writ respondents to release the unused 0.75 acre of land appertaining to SA Plot No.1141 acquired under LA Case No.4 of 1977-78 Barishal in favour of the writ petitioners on refunding the actual compensation money as paid earlier to the title holder/the predecessor of the writ petitioners at the time of acquisition. 

 "8. Release from Requisition—(1) Where any requisitioned property is to be released from requisition the Deputy Commissioner may restore it to the persons from whom the property was requisitioned or to his successor-in-interest or to such other persons as may appear to the Deputy Commissioner to be entitled to such restoration. 

 (2) The delivery of possession of the requisitioned property to the person referred to in sub-section (1) shall be a full discharge of the Deputy Commissioner from all liability in respect of such delivery, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect of the property which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom possession of the property is so delivered: 

 (4) When a notice referred to in sub-section (3) is published in the Official Gazette, the property specified in such notice shall cease to be subject to requisition on and from the date of such publication and be deemed to have been delivered to the person entitled to possession thereof; and the Deputy Commissioner shall not be liable for any compensation or other claim in respect of the property for any period after the said date. 

 16. On perusal of the aforesaid provisions of law it appears that the power to release any property is, from requisition, not from acquisition, which has been given under the above mentioned law upon the Deputy Commissioner which is a discretionary power and the discretion is to be exercised only when a thing necessary for any person from whom the property has been requisition to be entitled to such restoration he may restore to such person or to his successor-in-interest. However, the provision of section 8 of the Requisition of Property Act applies only in respect of requisition not acquisition. 8B. Withdrawal from Acquisition—When the owner of any property which has been acquired under section 5 is willing to receive back the property, the Government may, at any time before the payment of compensation, withdraw from the acquisition of any such property by notification published in the Official Gazette, and on such withdrawal, the property shall be restored to the possession of the owner, and with effect from the date of such restoration, the property shall vest back in the owner with the rights which he had before such property was acquired." 

 19. Furthermore, from the record of LA Case No.4 of 1977-78 as submitted before us through additional paper book dated 22-10-2018 it is clearly divulged that the awardee/ title holder has already received the compensation and on 2-12-1978 possession of the land had already been handed over to requiring body. 

 24. In the case of Al-haj Abul Bashar being dead his heirs Hosne Ara Begum vs Bangladesh reported in 50 DLR (AD) 11 this Division has also observed that—"from the Inter-Ministerial Communications it appears that the Ministry of Land Administration directed the Secretaries of various departments of Bangladesh that unutilized requisitioned land may be returned to the original owners, if not required. These Inter-Ministerial Communications only lay down the policy of the Government which the various Government departments shall follow in the case of unutilized requisitioned land. These Inter-Ministerial Communications are merely policy guidelines as to how the excess and unutilized lands are to be treated but these instructions do not create any legal right in favour of the petitioners to ask for return of the land from the Government after the same has been validly requisitioned under the law. It is also on record that CDA with the approval of the Government had already completed the project for distributing plots to the low-paid employees and, as such, in reality it cannot be said that the land is not being utilized. Mere non-use of the land for years will not give any right to the petitioners. We also find that after completing all necessary formalities the land had already been handed over to the requiring body, namely, CDA. Since no legal or vested right has accrued in favour of the petitioners by mere Inter-Ministerial Communications the petitioners cannot have any legal right to ask for return of the land". 

 27. Therefore, the contentions advanced by Mr Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Senior Counsel referring the provision of section 5(7) of the Requisition of the Property Act pointed that since the final gazette notification has not yet been published, therefore, the aforesaid land in question has not been finally acquired and no title has vest with the Government. Therefore, according to section 8 of the Act, the property in question can be released by the Government are completely devoid of legal propositions. 

 29. In view of the above discussions and authority cited herein above it is crystal clear that once a property is acquired and vested in the Government after making payment of compensation there is no scope to release the same to the original owner or to his heirs.
